author: BranchM
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

author: Solofunk
quoted_text:
Hot take: private credit is the best RWA to hold and the worst one to borrow against.

@PanteraCapital showed in their latest report that it's already the most used RWA in DeFi, with 44.7% of it sitting in DeFi protocols.

Here's why that's risky: 
1) DeFi lending relies on selling collateral fast when loans go bad. 
2) Private credit exits through redemptions that can take weeks and get gated in a crunch.
3) So when collateral needs to be sold, liquidations fail and bad debt piles up.
4) The USDC lenders who thought they were earning "safe" yield are the ones left holding it.

Liquidity is still an issue for some RWAs, especially private credit. I'd be really careful looping it, it's probably not worth it for a few extra % APR.

Not every asset is meant to be looped or leveraged.

Publishing v0.57 on @huggingface now. 

This full version is the first Zeno model whose confident-failure warning beats a tuned gradient-boosted model on both held-out periods. That is the hardest comparator we run.

What's new on it:

 • ONNX and safetensors files for all 6 trained copies of the model, plus the original PyTorch files. Every ONNX file gives the same answers as the original, with a difference under 0.0000005.

 • Official size: 9,160,161 parameters (9.16M). Design: 6 layers, width 320, 8 heads, plus a part that reads each forecaster's past record. Trained on @NVIDIA L40S.

 • Instructions and inputs vs outputs: a short ONNX example that runs on a normal computer, with no GPU or PyTorch needed. A table explains each input (the forecasters, their past records, how often pairs of them missed together, which source) and each output (the chance each forecaster is confidently wrong, and the correction to the forecast). There's also a backtest lookup tool and the hosted API/MCP.

 • Technical details file: the model's settings in the standard Hugging Face format, plus the exact training code and the run certificate.

author: josephdelong
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

谁能赚到钱，谁能拿到结果。

上一代 OG 可以靠挖矿、ICO、攒项目、早期囤币，完成从普通人到大佬的阶级跃迁。

那今天刚进场的年轻人呢？

这些红利早就都没了。

现在一个没有资本、没有资源、没有早期筹码的普通人，想在币圈拿到一个大结果，最现实的一条路是什么？

做流量。

把自己变成流量。

把注意力变成影响力，再把影响力变成钱。

从这个角度看，Evelyn其实很聪明。

她选的可能恰恰是这个阶段，为数不多还能让一个新人快速向上爬的路。

而且很多人就算想复制，也复制不了。

因为你未必有她的履历，未必有她的外向性格，未必愿意高频社交，更未必有把自己长期放在聚光灯下被人议论的表达欲。

你准备靠什么在这个圈子里拿到结果？

你今天可以捧着手机笑她。

text:
Delivering personal agents to consumers will be infinitely more challenging than previous AI product categories. However, I do believe the value we can deliver (as an industry) is enormous.

Eras of recent AI history (as I see them):

1. 2022 - chatGPT (thought partner, novel, fun)
2. 2024 - coding harness (powerful, real economic value)
3. 2025/6 - work harnesses (coding harness w/ veneer)
4. 2026 - personal agent harness (coding harness w/ plugins, its own VM w/ computer & browser use)

#4 will be BY FAR the most challenging to deliver to customers. #1 chatGPT was received as a delightful, non-threatening chat bot. #2/#3 was embraced by developers and tinkerers alike, and the net-new capabilities were impossible to ignore. Enterprises supported this push as well. 

Personal agents do have the ultimate promise of AGI as we know it. But to actually deliver this value (as an industry), we need to navigate the cold embrace of consumers, who are:

- leery of granting access to their personal data to AI companies (a prerequisite for personal agent success)
- feeling threatened by the industry as a whole
- unimpressed by content showcasing capability over value

This is an exciting challenge, and will require extreme empathy towards our end customers to be done right.

This is ridiculously useful.

Ai2 built an 8-billion-parameter AI for writing cited research reports.

Then released the weights, training data, and a workflow for your own PDFs.

You shouldn’t need a giant lab’s resources to start making sense of the literature.

Meet AstaBrief:

• Give it a research question and relevant paper excerpts. It turns them into a structured report with citations you can check.

• It powers Fast mode in Asta, averaging 51.1 seconds per report versus 178.5 seconds for the Claude-powered Thinking mode. Roughly 3.5× faster across the full workflow.

• It writes the report in one pass, skipping several slower processing stages.

• The model builds on Qwen3-8B, with training focused on relevant answers and citations that support the claims.

• Researchers can adapt the included PDF workflow and run report generation on their own infrastructure. Useful when the question itself reveals unpublished work.

Most evaluations were conducted in 2025, so this isn’t a claim that it beats today’s best models.

It’s something more practical: a specialized research tool you can download and build on.

Less time assembling a first report.

More time deciding what’s worth investigating.

text:
Aave is expanding both sides of its lending business:

> who supplies capital
> what borrowers can use as collateral

Just look at the recent launches.

Tokenized stocks bring a new source of borrowing demand, as investors can retain their equity exposure while borrowing stablecoins against it.

@Dialectic_Group's seven stock vaults, built on @makinafi, take that a step further: use the equities as collateral on @Aave, deploy the borrowed USDC into yield strategies, and pass the spread back to depositors.

Same with @superformxyz's Earn Stocks.

The investor gets yield on their tokenized stocks while Aave gets borrowing activity and revenue.

V4 expands how far this can go. Markets can accommodate different assets, access requirements and risk parameters while sharing liquidity within a hub. That gives institutions more flexibility to build credit products around their own requirements.

We're already seeing public companies like @Securitize proposing to deploy tokenized funds on Aave, and top curators like @SentoraHQ proposing to deploy their own lending markets on V4.

On the supply side, Aave App and integrations into wallets and financial products open new distribution channels for capital.

A user saving dollars through a familiar app can become a supplier to Aave without ever interacting with a lending dashboard. Banks and fintechs will very likely embed these products and extend that distribution to their existing customers. Banks/fintechs still own the relationship with users, and Aave gets the underlying deposits.

GHO adds yet another source of revenue through borrowing and the yield generated by GSM reserves. As its use expands across savings, payments and collateral markets, more of that financial activity can contribute to the DAO's economics. @ether_fi, for example, proposed to incorporate GHO as a spending currency. This would be a big catalyst.

All of these developments reinforce each other.

Broader distribution brings capital, more collateral types bring borrowers, and more borrowers bring revenue.

That's why I'm bullish on $AAVE: an established lending business expanding into securities finance, consumer savings and institutional credit, with more ways to generate revenue from the activity it supports.

quoted_text:
Quick refresher on what HaloGuard actually does, because a lot has changed.

HaloGuard sits around an AI agent and does two jobs. It checks everything going in before the agent ever sees it, and it checks everything coming out before the agent is allowed to act on it.

Every input checked, every output governed.

Here's where it stands today:
• The input guard is live and SOTA, screening prompts, documents and anything an agent reads and stopping attacks before they land, and it's peer-reviewed, published on arXiv and top of its class at a fraction of the size of the models it beats
 • The output guard checks every response and action before it executes, and it's climbing fast, from 73.9% to 81.87% F1 and a few points from SOTA
 • It doesn't just scan for bad words, it understands what a request is really trying to do, so a harmful request disguised as an innocent one still gets caught
 • It covers 46 languages, so an attack written in Arabic or Mandarin gets the same scrutiny as one in English
 • It runs inline in under 100ms, so protection never slows the agent down
 • It's open weights, so anyone can download it, inspect it and test it, no black box

And it keeps getting better because of the network behind it. Every week, miners on SN23 are paid to break HaloGuard, and every attack that gets through becomes training data that makes the next one harder.

Agents are reading more, touching more and acting on their own every month. HaloGuard makes sure what goes in is safe and what comes out is approved, before anything happens.

text:
Thanks @168X_Fortune and @168MrZ for having me back. Here is the summary in English

TLDR, AI fundamentals are still getting stronger. But after the big run, I’m keeping positions light and waiting for a cleaner setup. The next major opportunity could be the assets that high rates have kept under pressure.

Here’s how I’m thinking about it:

1. US10Y: volatility matters more than the exact yield.

I’m less concerned about whether the 10-year yield is 5.3% or 5.5% than how violently it moves. Before adding meaningful risk, I want yields stabilizing or gradually declining, with MOVE—the bond market’s volatility index—coming down too.

2. Market breadth needs to resolve.

Money has concentrated in AI winners while much of the market struggles. Breadth can improve through laggards catching up, or through winners correcting. Either outcome makes chasing semiconductors with maximum size less attractive here.

3. The catch-up basket: KRE, IWM, RKT and XLU.

Regional banks, small caps, housing and utilities could respond sharply to easing rate pressure, helped by short covering. The condition matters: an orderly decline in yields supports that setup. A sudden collapse could signal recession instead.

4. Mid term election is not a risk to AI datacenter development.
The key topics from Democrats are still inflation, Iran and gas price. These have higher priority than AI datacenter. However I see long term risk as the US people's sentiment towards AI and datacenter is quickly deteriorate except people who are working in the AI industry.

5. The oil issue extends beyond crude.

Refinery capacity and refined-product supply deserve more attention. Having crude available doesn’t automatically solve gasoline or diesel shortages. Persistent pressure on those products can keep inflation expectations—and long-term yields—elevated.

6. AI revenue growth is the key validation.

I’m skeptical of claims that OpenAI is already at $70B ARR. But if coding and enterprise growth stays steep, an $80–100B annualized revenue run rate by year-end is conceivable. That’s a possible outcome, not a confirmed number. Downstream revenue must justify upstream capex.

7. Google’s biggest opportunity is a personal AI agent.

Google has distribution through Search, YouTube, Gmail, Maps and Android, existing monetization infrastructure, and its own hardware-to-model stack with low inference cost. I’d like to see it combine those advantages into a personal agent. Coding isn't its advantage.

8. The next AI re-rating needs evidence of returns.

Personal agents, AI for Science, biotech and enterprise applications could broaden monetization beyond coding. Faster research, cheaper drug discovery and measurable productivity gains would help demonstrate that AI spending can generate attractive returns on invested capital.

9. AI IPOs could redistribute the premium.

If OpenAI or Anthropic goes public, investors would gain direct access to another layer of AI monetization. Some capital could rotate away from semiconductor proxies. That could change where the AI premium sits even while chip fundamentals remain healthy.

10. I’m more selective within semiconductors.

CPU still has catch-up potential as server architecture evolves. Optical has already run hard, and strong memory results may already be well understood. I’m treating semiconductor equipment more tactically. Timing matters increasingly after the sector’s major advance.

11. BTC is my first watch when the rate setup improves.

If US10Y and MOVE genuinely top out, BTC looks like a strong expression of improving liquidity and risk appetite. Its technical structure matters too. I’d look at that strength alongside the catch-up potential in rate-sensitive equities.

12. TLT calls have become less attractive.

High bond volatility makes options expensive. Even if TLT rises as yields decline, falling implied volatility can eat into call returns. For this setup, I prefer considering equities with underlying businesses that could benefit from easing rate pressure.

13. My main macro catalysts: FOMC, CPI and Treasury issuance.

These can change expectations for policy, inflation and long-term bond supply. For the midterms, I care most about what follows: changes to fiscal policy and issuance that could alter the path of long-term yields.

14. Light positioning is a deliberate choice.

I already traded the post-September FOMC rally aggressively. Now I’m waiting for better risk/reward. With leverage and options, timing matters enormously. A stable index can still hide severe drawdowns in individual stocks.

15. The next big trade could be the laggards catching up.

I remain confident in AI’s fundamentals, especially as downstream monetization expands. But confidence doesn’t require maximum exposure at every price. If yields stabilize and MOVE falls, BTC and KRE/IWM/RKT/XLU could offer a compelling next setup.

For now, I’m keeping risk light, watching the bond market, and waiting for the opportunity to become clearer.

text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

Henri Kagan’s path to scientific greatness was anything but straightforward.
Born near Paris in 1930, his childhood was shaped by World War II, when his family sought refuge in southern France under assumed names. Back at school, Kagan recalled being “not what you would call a good student.” He began on a literary track before discovering his fascination with mathematics, physics and chemistry.

The road remained bumpy:
he initially planned to become an engineer and failed his first entrance exam to chemistry school. He tried again, and succeeded.
That persistence and curiosity eventually helped Kagan become a pioneer of asymmetric catalysis, transforming scientists’ ability to create chiral molecules.

In 2001, Kagan shared the Wolf Prize in Chemistry with Ryoji Noyori and K. Barry Sharpless.
As Kagan later said: “One of the interests of research is to go toward the unknown, and to be attentive to the unexpected.”

A fitting description of his own journey.

Historical details (including the Ice Box design) show cold keys are recovered only to sign a withdrawal, after which remaining funds move to a fresh address so the private key is never reused. text:
Impressive work from the recent math drops, the unit-distance counterexample, the sub-n log n multiplication result, and the 3SUM/APSP improvements are genuinely humbling for prior intuitions.

That said, treating a classical ECDSA break in months as a planning baseline still looks like FUD. 

A practical private-key recovery attack on secp256k1 (or similar curves) on available hardware would not stay confined to Bitcoin and Ethereum. It would compromise TLS, code signing, most banking systems, and a large fraction of deployed public-key infrastructure at once. 

Hash-based schemes are attractive precisely because they minimize algebraic structure, but the same loss of mathematical intuition that motivates caution on curves also applies to hashes ;-)

A calm hygiene improvement (avoiding address reuse after the first signature) is reasonable for large holders, and all good wallets incentivizes using new addresses. 

But calling for a “mass migration” would create operational mistakes that lose funds with higher probability than the scenario being mitigated.

We already have a Post Quantum migration to execute, let's not add more confusion.

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

The policy goal should be an open, interoperable payment layer, with safeguards that match the risks—not closed marketplaces that decide who can participate.

text:
Huge congratulations to @NousResearch and team @dillonrolnick @Teknium @karan4d @theemozilla @gradyacc and many others on closing their $90M Series B at a $1.5B valuation. @Delphi_Ventures co-led their seed round, doubled down in their Series A, and participated again here. This marks us tripling down on Nous.

Following Nous' journey over the past few years has recalibrated my view of top tier founders

The team has always been months to years ahead at every juncture. They did synthetic model evaluations years before people got sick of benchmark maxing, distributed training runs before it was interesting, YARN to massively increase context length back when you couldn't dump endless text into LLMs and millions of downloads for their fine tuned Hermes Models. There were also a lot of fun projects along the way like WorldSim (massive world simulation) and FORGE.

Fast forward to today and there are 24M+ downloads of Hermes Agent since February, #1 among apps on OpenRouter by daily token usage, and 250,000+ GitHub stars along with just mass virality. The Nous team estimates Hermes drives approximately 2.5% of all global token usage.

Nous has created two things that I think are both foundational and sticky

First, Nous created a religion and an authentic cult like following. They achieved this through grassroots interest and involvement from their community and users, and by actually embracing them. A recurring example is Teknium replying to users at all hours of the day, working with them and integrating their pull requests into Hermes agent. The project’s ethos is open source and against a totalitarian end state where a room full of folks controls AI and reality itself, and that resonates globally.

The second reason is that Hermes agent unlocks a fundamental new spot on the AI optimization frontier as the open source non lab owned option. Every major competitor is owned by an AI lab (Muse owned by Meta, OpenClaw by OpenAI, Grok by SpaceX, Instinct which is closed source). With Hermes Agent you own everything you create around an AI model so you have that as a long term evolving asset (Business or personal) instead of getting IP farmed

Also with Hermes agent you can drive differentiated outcomes versus using the same model as everyone else. Individuals and businesses have a comprehensive set of owned depth around the model (Evaluations, memory, interactions, data, private IP, variety of open or closed or fine tuned models, and more). This lends itself to an AI agent that grows with you that you own for life. 

Both @satyanadella and @PalantirTech’s have shared this view that corporations don’t want to give away their IP anymore and be farmed. They want to own it as an asset.

I’ve shared my full thesis on this concept of owning vs renting your intelligence here: https://t.co/cW05wedLRD

Hermes Agent is not just a random spark, it’s the result of a team that has spent years building products, building systems and being fully enveloped in the AI world. The thousands of micro decisions and the culmination of the team led to Hermes Agent.

So what comes next? 

When you have tens of millions of users already, they can become the champions within a business to bring their Hermes build to all employees of a company. They can start sharing skills, interactions, interop, data and more and build something truly multiplayer for enterprise. 

Having Nvidia, Microsoft and Samsung as investors doubles as enabling them to be extremely smart in potentially onboarding a massive enterprise user base to Hermes Enterprise. This isn't just private businesses using Hermes internally; it's Fortune 500 companies who can offer customized and unique agents to their customers and users built on Hermes Enterprise. 

Hermes' agent was not built to be a casual or fleeting personal agent and this lends itself to a larger business expansion. 

As Teknium shared 

“I fully intend and have plainly stated many times that I always built hermes to be the most powerful AI Agent. "Normie" consumers can leverage that and we do what we can to make it an experience they can approach (the mobile app will be almost exclusively focused on consumer) - but they are not our only demographic. I want the scientists, the cybersecurity engineers, the developers, the knowledge workers, the creatives, and everyone else to be able to have an agent that they can leverage that is maximally useful to them too.…”

Nous has captured the hearts and minds of the smartest user base on earth and that's the wedge. 

Nous is building for a future where you have sovereignty over your AI stack. They are the center of gravity for Open source AI developers, users, investors and supporters. 

The AI discussion has been dominated by fear mongering driven by centralized labs to obtain a regulatory moat. This is very obvious. The safest path in my opinion is open source and acceleration. An entire world of agents pressure testing, building and dealing with each other aligned to the individual vs aligned to a centralized team of decision makers at a lab. Nous is the answer. Nous has now raised $158M to date to execute this vision.

Internally we have people who have built insane Hermes agent builds including @KSimback and @pierskicks. I have built an insanely deep Hermes build that takes in 40+ private and public data sources and finds me new founders to invest in, helps manage my liquid portfolio, and tracks my entire historical journey as a VC (past founders, deals, much more).

A few fun content items through the years has been our AMA with Teknium and our Podcast with Jeff

Tarun is extremely deep on AI, inference (see his latest article) and open source and is the ideal lead investor in Nous.

Also amped for the Hermes Mobile App

Our goal at Delphi Ventures is to be the biggest supporters and investors of our portfolio companies. We are extremely excited for the future of Nous.

text:
This might be the biggest opportunity blockchains have ever had. 

Technology has mostly been built around durable yet centralized trust systems. But the factors acting against these systems are getting more powerful as we near Super Intelligence™️. 

Obviously code can break due to the sheer mathematical progress AI is bringing, but less obviously, humans can be broken too. Impersonation, blackmail, and other forms of social engineering attacks are only going to get more advanced. As such, just fixing holes in code made to secure our lives is not enough, to build truly trustworthy systems of value, you will have to decentralize them and add immutability such that no single actor can, in most clear words, “not fuck it up.” This is exactly what Ethereum was built for. 

“Alright man, so what is Ethereum doing to survive this age? Are we cooked?”

Quite the contrary, the frontier is moving fast, but Ethereum is moving faster. Some quick points: 

1. The Hegotá upgrade will set the tone. 

This upgrade will make Ethereum cryptographically agile. 

EIP-8141, lovingly known as “Frames,” changes Ethereum accounts at the root level so that transaction validations can be programmable instead of tied to the ECSDA key (the thing Justin is warning people about in his post). Essentially accounts can choose how to authenticate instead of being tied to the current status quo. There are a few quantum proof signatures out there like ML-DSA and SPHINCS, with frames you can choose whatever and also be open to even more gigabrain ones to come. When you are faced with a threat, agility is key, and Hegotá sets the tone for that agility.

2. The J* upgrade will produce a MVP quantum proof L1. 

Okay, I know what you’re thinking, “why would you ever name such a consequential thing ‘I*’???What is wrong with you??” Trust me I thought this too, but I was promptly educated that names are not finalized until we get closer, in fact, the names even get a fun emoji next to them (e.g The Hegotá upgrade emoji is a goat 🐐 IFYKYK :P)

ANYWAYS

Think of J* as answering “what are the minimal changes Ethereum needs to make if quantum computers exist tomorrow?”  

The goal here is to have enough to survive Q-day. Today, this maps to achieving a PQ heartbeat on consenus layers, leanDA PQ sampling, and leanSPHINCS transactions on execution. 

TLDR: the aim is to ship this and then play Alright by Kendrick shortly after: “we gon’ be alright!” 

4. The boxes are moving in real time 

If you’ve ever seen the strawmap (a proposed roadmap for Ethereum), you’ll know it has a lot of boxes. In particular, there is a quantum box. Also fun fact: it’s literally called a strawmap because it moves as research moves, and man is it moving! 

> On August 12, leanVM was moved forward from J* to I*
> A week later, the roadmap added the minimal viable post-quantum L1 milestone to J* 

If you’re ever wondering whether Ethereum is taking this seriously, just watch the boxes and see how they dance. 

5. AI is actually HELPING

AI makes cryptographic research faster, and AI assisted formal verification means you don’t have to trust AI’s answer. Check out some of @fradamt’s posts for more. 

6. Quantum is just one threat in a much bigger battle 

You can quantum proof a bank’s system but still be fallible to the humans that run it. Ethereum tackles this from both sides, it gardens the security while also distributing the authors of the network such that there is no single point of attack.

Other blockchains, and any place that stores value TBH, will begin to claim they are quantum proof, but they fail to address the threat of being human proof too. 

7. The grand prize is here, and Ethereum can grab it. 

A neutral and secure place for ALL value, that cannot be coerced by a government, a company, or Superintelligence. 

Your life, your story, your money, can be here, forever. And many generations from now, the kids will look up and think: thank god they tried. 

Godspeed. 

Ethereum.

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

Doomerism has now hit cryptography...

Unfortunately, on reflection, I think this is a very sober call. No reason to be taking unnecessary risk with all of the rapid progress happening in mathematics. The risk is not quantum, but just conventional mathematics overturning unproven cryptographic hardness assumptions.

It's UTXO-mode for a while.

text:
People are surprised that AI is finding weird unelegant maths results like this. I think there is a plausible explanation.

Maths (and adjacent disciplines like physics and comp sci) had elegant results so far because humans are biased towards elegant solutions. I think this bias is due to how human minds work. We have a pretty small context window, and we are only able to find solutions that are relatively elegant.

This gave us the impression that maths and the universe are elegant. Maybe they are not, and we are now finding out because we have intelligences that can work with much more complex solutions.

text:
After listening to Jeff's DAS interview, my $DRV bull thesis is unchanged, and possibly strengthened. 

No, this isn't cope. Strap in for a long one.

First off, it was framed in a terribly misleading way by CoinTelegraph for clickbait (shocking).

Jeff was asked if we he wasn't forced to be focused on perps infra, their core business, and was instead a 3rd party builder, what would he find interesting to build.

His answer was that he'd look for whatever hadn't really been built yet, and mentioned options as a good example. He then added that they're tremendously important as an instrument in TradFi, so figuring out why that hasn't translated over to crypto would be an interesting problem to solve. 

He then added that HIP4 is already their attempt at building the infrastructure to allow teams to build options on @HyperliquidX. There are dozens of teams building binary options already using HIP4 infrastructure. There are several teams building vanilla options on top of Hyperliquid already. None of these products have taken a meaningful bite out of @DeriveXYZ market dominance yet, and they are live right now.

He didn't say that they were building options in house, he just said that someone should build options on chain because there's a massive gap between the success and traction they've had on chain vs in TradFi. This is extremely validating of the $DRV thesis.

People need to realize and remember that @DeriveXYZ wasn't specifically written off for all these years, the entire sector of on chain options was deemed as impossible and uninvestable. We've heard, "Options can't exist on chain, options are obsoleted by perps, no retail crypto traders will learn to trade options, etc etc". Jeff negated all of the FUD that on chain options have received over the years and basically said it was the place to be right now.

Jeff did specifically say that no on chain options protocol has reached "escape velocity" yet. So if you read between the lines, he's basically saying that on chain options are interesting and necessary as a tool, that they're nascent in their growth as compared to TradFi TAM, and that it's one of the most interesting spots of the market to be focused on building right now. $DRV pumping 10x and having insane hockey stick volume growth YTD isn't "escape velocity" in his eyes, and he's right. $DRV is still cheap and early relative to the market it's expanding into. Job's not finished by any means.

It's important to highlight that unlike Vlad from @Lighter_xyz who explicitly says they are building options in house, Jeff said nothing of the sort. Hyperliquid sees themselves as building the neutral infrastructure layers of liquidity for builders to come and build on top of. Look at TradeXYZ and HIP3. He didn't say that they hired a team of 20 ex-Optiver and ex-SIG guys to be their internal options trading desk, he didn't insinuate a launch date, he didn't say HIP-5 is vanilla options. He basically said, "On-chain options are cool and underexplored, I hope teams come and build them on top of our existing infra". 

Sidenote, I actually think his description of priority fees was actually way more signal and very bullish $HYPE. Way more bullish priority fee growth and obviously AQAv2 fees than anything HIP4 related.

At the end of the day, none of what he said is new information. I always have stated in my $DRV bullposts that they will not maintain their current 90%+ market share in 2027. This is an entire primitive that does quadrillions of dollars in volume in TradFi. The on chain pie will grow massively. There will inevitably be more competition for that pie.  $DRV could lose half their market share to @Lighter_xyz and @HyperliquidX and still be cheap here at these prices when on chain options volume 10x's or more.

I'd also like to point out the irony that I'm long $HYPE and $LIT calls on @DeriveXYZ right now, and I still can't long $DRV perps on Lighter or Hyperliquid. 

I just refuse to subscribe to this notion that I should sell a phenomenal asset today because maybe there will be competition tomorrow, or next month, or next year. When they have live products, I'll reaccess the situation. Until then, competing against non-existent products that are just presumed to be superior is an unfair standard that seemingly only $DRV gets held to, and irrational selloffs like today, especially based off misleading headlines, are just better entries for me in the long run.

We're excited to invest in Preference Model.

Building RL environments that actually work is harder than it looks. Models are relentless at reward hacking, finding shortcuts, and exploiting vulnerabilities.

@preferencemodel has focused on the domain that matters most to labs right now: AI research and ML engineering itself.

Over the past year, the team has built RL environments for leading labs. Their focus has been on building the infrastructure to make harder, more resistant environments as models improve: tooling that finds where models are weak, generates new tasks to target those gaps, and tests environments against agents actively trying to break it.

This week they're open-sourcing Karotte, the framework they've used in production — hardened through more than a million evaluation runs and red-teaming.

We're thrilled to partner with @chem_safety and @Ning_Catsnail and the Preference Model team as they build the training grounds for capable and aligned models.

By @JenniferHli

Huge congratulations to @NousResearch and team @dillonrolnick @Teknium @karan4d @theemozilla @gradyacc and many others on closing their $90M Series B at a $1.5B valuation. @Delphi_Ventures co-led their seed round, doubled down in their Series A, and participated again here. This marks us tripling down on Nous.

Following Nous' journey over the past few years has recalibrated my view of top tier founders

The team has always been months to years ahead at every juncture. They did synthetic model evaluations years before people got sick of benchmark maxing, distributed training runs before it was interesting, YARN to massively increase context length back when you couldn't dump endless text into LLMs and millions of downloads for their fine tuned Hermes Models. There were also a lot of fun projects along the way like WorldSim (massive world simulation) and FORGE.

Fast forward to today and there are 24M+ downloads of Hermes Agent since February, #1 among apps on OpenRouter by daily token usage, and 250,000+ GitHub stars along with just mass virality. The Nous team estimates Hermes drives approximately 2.5% of all global token usage.

Nous has created two things that I think are both foundational and sticky

First, Nous created a religion and an authentic cult like following. They achieved this through grassroots interest and involvement from their community and users, and by actually embracing them. A recurring example is Teknium replying to users at all hours of the day, working with them and integrating their pull requests into Hermes agent. The project’s ethos is open source and against a totalitarian end state where a room full of folks controls AI and reality itself, and that resonates globally.

The second reason is that Hermes agent unlocks a fundamental new spot on the AI optimization frontier as the open source non lab owned option. Every major competitor is owned by an AI lab (Muse owned by Meta, OpenClaw by OpenAI, Grok by SpaceX, Instinct which is closed source). With Hermes Agent you own everything you create around an AI model so you have that as a long term evolving asset (Business or personal) instead of getting IP farmed

Also with Hermes agent you can drive differentiated outcomes versus using the same model as everyone else. Individuals and businesses have a comprehensive set of owned depth around the model (Evaluations, memory, interactions, data, private IP, variety of open or closed or fine tuned models, and more). This lends itself to an AI agent that grows with you that you own for life. 

Both @satyanadella and @PalantirTech’s have shared this view that corporations don’t want to give away their IP anymore and be farmed. They want to own it as an asset.

I’ve shared my full thesis on this concept of owning vs renting your intelligence here: https://t.co/cW05wedLRD

Hermes Agent is not just a random spark, it’s the result of a team that has spent years building products, building systems and being fully enveloped in the AI world. The thousands of micro decisions and the culmination of the team led to Hermes Agent.

So what comes next? 

When you have tens of millions of users already, they can become the champions within a business to bring their Hermes build to all employees of a company. They can start sharing skills, interactions, interop, data and more and build something truly multiplayer for enterprise. 

Having Nvidia, Microsoft and Samsung as investors doubles as enabling them to be extremely smart in potentially onboarding a massive enterprise user base to Hermes Enterprise. This isn't just private businesses using Hermes internally; it's Fortune 500 companies who can offer customized and unique agents to their customers and users built on Hermes Enterprise. 

Hermes' agent was not built to be a casual or fleeting personal agent and this lends itself to a larger business expansion. 

As Teknium shared 

“I fully intend and have plainly stated many times that I always built hermes to be the most powerful AI Agent. "Normie" consumers can leverage that and we do what we can to make it an experience they can approach (the mobile app will be almost exclusively focused on consumer) - but they are not our only demographic. I want the scientists, the cybersecurity engineers, the developers, the knowledge workers, the creatives, and everyone else to be able to have an agent that they can leverage that is maximally useful to them too.…”

Nous has captured the hearts and minds of the smartest user base on earth and that's the wedge. 

Nous is building for a future where you have sovereignty over your AI stack. They are the center of gravity for Open source AI developers, users, investors and supporters. 

The AI discussion has been dominated by fear mongering driven by centralized labs to obtain a regulatory moat. This is very obvious. The safest path in my opinion is open source and acceleration. An entire world of agents pressure testing, building and dealing with each other aligned to the individual vs aligned to a centralized team of decision makers at a lab. Nous is the answer. Nous has now raised $158M to date to execute this vision.

Internally we have people who have built insane Hermes agent builds including @KSimback and @pierskicks. I have built an insanely deep Hermes build that takes in 40+ private and public data sources and finds me new founders to invest in, helps manage my liquid portfolio, and tracks my entire historical journey as a VC (past founders, deals, much more).

A few fun content items through the years has been our AMA with Teknium and our Podcast with Jeff 

AMA: https://t.co/XeeB8WdTEv

Podcast: https://t.co/wM6RQqHw94

Very excited for @robotventures (@tarunchitra and @rleshner) to lead the round alongside @nvidia @Microsoft @Samsung @usv (@fredwilson), @MenloVentures (@deedydas and team), @ycombinator and @1789Capital. Tarun is extremely deep on AI, inference (see his latest article) and open source and is the ideal lead investor in Nous.

Also amped for the Hermes Mobile App

Our goal at Delphi Ventures is to be the biggest supporters and investors of our portfolio companies. We are extremely excited for the future of Nous.

For a datachain, the maximum rate of data ingress is almost the whole ballgame. That ceiling decides which use cases the chain can support.

Onchain backups sound like a nice use case? 

Not at 1 TB of max ingress a day. That is 10 photo libraries, 2 laptop images, or one 4K project. 

If your total ingress is 1 TB a day, you’re an archive, not a backup network.

Had to explain it to a few folks, apparently it helps understanding the argument better.

- Elliptic cryptography (used in almost all blockchains) is built on clever tricks and fancy math assumptions, an engineering analogy would be self-stressed structures
- AI labs breaking math assumptions left and right lately, might break elliptic crypto too (maybe already did!)
- Better use something dumb and straightforward, more like solid concrete bricks, like hash-based cryptography

Coincidentally it would also be post-quantum safe but it's not the point.
author: toly
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
So you are telling me an Ethereum researcher is warning Bitcoin whales to enter “bunker mode”?

Justin Drake just published one of the strangest Bitcoin warnings I’ve seen in a while.

And no man, Bitcoin hasn’t been hacked.

But the scenario he’s describing is much worse if it ever becomes real.

The idea:

Bitcoin relies on elliptic-curve cryptography to protect private keys

today, deriving a private key from a public key is computationally impractical

Drake is preparing for a world where that assumption suddenly stops being true

AI could accelerate mathematical discoveries, quantum computing could eventually use Shor’s algorithm against elliptic curves

or, in the extreme scenario, someone discovers a classical equivalent capable of doing something similar without a quantum computer

Drake defines the nightmare pretty clearly:

recovering a private key from a public key in ONE WEEK using commercially available hardware like a large GPU cluster.

If that happens, things get ugly very quickly.

Really really ugly

Because not every Bitcoin is equally exposed.

many Bitcoin addresses initially reveal only a hash of the public key

some very old Bitcoin outputs sent directly to public keys have been exposed for years
Taproot has different public-key exposure characteristics

billions of dollars in old BTC could suddenly become interesting targets

This is why Drake is talking about “bunker mode.”

His recommendation is basically prepare before everyone realizes they need to prepare.

- move important funds gradually to fresh addresses
- avoid address reuse
- prefer addresses that have never signed a transaction
- after spending, move the remaining balance to another fresh address
- rotate critical keys

And most importantly: DON’T PANIC.

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
To paraphrase an old Soviet joke

Newsom is visiting a [insert functional state], and the central committee secretary offers to fly him around the city on his jet.  It’s a super nice gulfstream 600.  Newsom asks the secretary, “how can you afford such a luxury as a public servant?”   

The secretary, after a few drinks, says “well, you see that 20 billion high speed rail down there? I rounded up a bunch of rural workers and worked them 9/9/6 and we built the rail 20% under budget”.  He then leans in and whispers, “I told the central committee it was 15% under budget”. 

A few years later the secretary is visiting Newsom.  Newsom offers to take him around on California on his jet.  It’s the top end gulfstream 2000.  The secretary asks the same question, and Newsom responds, “Can you see that $100 billion high speed rail I campaigned for?”  The secretary answers, “no i don’t”. Newsom leans in and says “exactly”.

author: Bookof_Eth
quoted_text:
This is Ethereum.

There are 291 projects, companies, protocols and communities in this image. It is still only a fraction of what has been built.

What makes this remarkable isn't just the scale. It's how that scale was created.

There is no parent company behind all of this. No CEO allocating capital across these projects, no central entity deciding who gets to build or what the ecosystem should become. Thousands of independent teams, communities and individuals have built their own piece of Ethereum, often with completely different goals, while sharing the same underlying infrastructure.

Finance, credit, stablecoins, payments, RWAs, privacy, identity, gaming, social applications, infrastructure, culture and public goods are increasingly becoming parts of the same composable economy.

That structure matters.

Value isn't concentrated in one company at the top. It is distributed across protocols, builders, users, communities and assets. Yet they can still reinforce each other because they share Ethereum as common infrastructure.

And underneath that economy sits ethereum:native.

ethereum:native  secures Ethereum, pays for its blockspace and is used throughout the ecosystem as collateral, liquidity and money. As more applications, assets and economic activity settle on Ethereum, the economic role of ETH grows with it.

This is why we believe ETH remains heavily undervalued.

The market often looks at ETH as another crypto asset. We look at what is actually being built around it.

291 logos in one image, with many more still missing. And most of the world's people, assets and economic activity haven't even moved onchain yet. 

Ethereum is no longer just an experiment in decentralized technology.

It is becoming an entire economy,  built by many, owned by no one, with ETH at its core.

BOOElieve in the future of Ethereum and ethereum:native

text:
These 0.99999984 solutions are not as "ugly" as it may seem.

The truth is, those are not the real runtimes of the algorithms published. To make the proof simpler, they use absurd safety bounds like 2^50 that are entirely arbitrary.

For example, imagine proving that 1/x^2 > 0. This proof is much harder if you include the area around x=0, as it blows up to infinity there. Instead, if you only prove it for x>=99999, it avoids this blowup and simplifies the proof, but still gets the point across.

The "real" bounds of those solutions are probably much tighter, maybe even something "beautiful" like O(n*lg lg n). But the goal of the AI papers was just to show that improvement is possible, not that the bounds are perfect (which is usually much harder to prove). Over the coming weeks and months, we'll likely see a lot of tightening.

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

quoted_text:
My account is finally back.

First, a security reminder: please use a unique, randomly generated strong password for every important account. Do not rely on 2FA alone. 2FA can be bypassed, and I strongly recommend using a passkey.

Here’s what happened:

On Sep 30, I received an email about a new login to my X account. Unfortunately, I didn’t pay enough attention to it at the time.

On Oct 1, my account was compromised despite having 2FA enabled. My Gmail account remained under my control the entire time, and I have never entered my credentials on any phishing/scam website. As far as I can determine, the attacker only had my password. How they managed to bypass 2FA and take over the account is still unclear to me.

About 10 minutes after the takeover — while I was still on vacation — I received an email from Kimbo Chen telling me that my account appeared to have been hacked. Huge thanks to him for noticing and reaching out so quickly.

When I checked, my password had already been changed and a large number of scam links had been sent through my Chats. What made the situation even worse was that the Chat passcode could apparently be reset directly, while I myself could no longer access my own Chats.

I immediately opened my first ticket with X Support. The initial response essentially said that because I could still access the account at that point, they would not take further action.

Later that same day, I lost all access to the account.

On Oct 6, I submitted another hacked-account ticket. The suspension on this account was subsequently lifted, but during this period @GenAI_is_real was targeted by the scam and nearly had their account compromised as well.

This whole situation was crazy.

Through the new support ticket, I was eventually able to reset the password and regain control of the account. The account is now back to normal.

I sincerely apologize for the impact caused by my poor security practices. More than 100 accounts were affected or contacted by the attacker, including @MIT_CSAIL (which has now blocked me), and @GenAI_is_real, who thankfully avoided losing their account.

I’m extremely grateful to everyone who warned me, helped report the account, or offered assistance during the past week. Special thanks again to Kimbo Chen, and to my colleague @frankyouchill for taking time out of an already busy schedule to help me deal with this mess.

Again: use unique random passwords, and use passkeys whenever possible. Treat 2FA as an additional layer of protection, not something that makes an account impossible to compromise.

Everything on this account should now be back to normal.

Thank you all for your help, and I hope everyone stays safe and has a great day.

It's the combination of a basis trade and funding capture.

Put simply: 

- Spot assets are bought when they are cheaper than their perp counterpart. The perp counterpart is being shorted.

- While the short is open, funding is collected. Funding rates can of course change, but long-term the vast majority of funding periods should pay you when being short given the traded tickers.

- An additional profit is realized when the pair is closed on sport-perp price convergence.

The strategy can trade every pair combination on Hyperliquid that is listed as SPOT and PERP asset, including HIP-3 markets. 

In practice however, markets like BTC or ETH will probably only be selected a few times a year as they are too efficient already. However, with new token listings appearing on a weekly basis, there is a constant opportunity across more illiquid books and mispriced markets.

If Hyperliquid continues to stay on its current growth trajectory and spot markets gaining further traction, the performance and capacity of this strategy can even increase in the future.

In the test month (see screenshot below), we were already running at a 50%+ APR, all while only having to deal with one exchange and not needing to spread our collateral across several DEXes to realize an opportunity.

If the % return comes down long-term to even half of that, it's still a massive win given the lack of bigger drawdowns.

We estimate the current TVL capacity for this strategy at somewhere around $5M before yields compress to <10%.

We are opening this strategy now to the public and will cap access at $2M combined TVL. 

Minimum is $1,000, maximum is $20,000 (higher amounts in your balance on Hyperliquid will be ignored and the strategy just treats it as $20,000).

As this strategy is purely focused on PNL, which is mainly created via funding payments, we won't even be earning enough via builder fees to cover the individual server costs per user.

- All preseed participants have access.
