text:
What to expect from $STATICS Phase 1.

Full DEX functionality.

Anyone can pay a creation fee and receive 5% of all pool hook fees for life from pools they create. For projects, this becomes a revenue stream for every pool they launch.

A new take on bribes and gauges.

Gauge rewards are continuously streamed to LPs who have in-range liquidity. Rewards are directed to pools by $STATICS stakers.

Stakers have a 4-hour cooldown once they allocate toward a pool. This kills JIT reward hopping while only requiring four hours before they can move their allocation again.

Anyone can fund up to four reward assets per pool and split those rewards at any desired ratio between pool LPs and gauge allocators.

If a project wants to attract gauge weight, it can fund allocator bribes. If it wants more LP liquidity, it can fund LP bribes. Or it can do both, using whatever split it chooses.

Imagine a single pool paying a memecoin, NVDA, WBTC, and WETH all as incentives.

And the best part?

The gauge rewards are not minted. They are funded by platform fees, buybacks, and existing token allocations.

No constant sell pressure from minting incentives.

$STATICS Staking.

You can stake your $STATICS tokens and give them two jobs during Phase 1.

Select up to 12 assets, and your weight will participate in each asset's global fee index.

Select USDG, for example, and get a cut of every swap fee paid in USDG, while doing the same across up to 12 different assets.

Choose a newer asset without much weight allocated to it? You earn more.

You can also allocate your stake weight toward any pool you choose, and that pool will receive a pro rata share of that period's gauge rewards, streamed continuously based on total allocated stake weight.

Example:

Pool A has 50 allocated stake.
Pool B has 20 allocated stake.
Pool C has 30 allocated stake.

There is 100 total stake allocated.

Pool A receives 50%.
Pool B receives 20%.
Pool C receives 30%.

Of course, bribes for allocators can greatly influence where that weight is directed.

One thing I want to mention is that Phase 1 will not include the ability to link an Operator NFT to a Position NFT and use activation weight to increase stake weight.

This functionality will be part of Phase 2, along with Basket Tokens.

Activation weight still matters because it applies to an Operator's fee-share weight from the main $STATICS pool.

Operators receive 40% of all trading fees from the main pool, and this will never change.

Only Operators will ever have a claim on the main pool's fees.

Overall, Phase 1 is a full-fledged DEX release with a new rewards system that takes inspiration from Aerodrome's new MetaDEX03 system.

It is just built on Uniswap v4 using hooks.

If you are an LP looking for new opportunities, keep an eye on us.

quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
Recent developments from frontier Physical AI companies are showing that robots are capable of moving from single task automation to complete workflow automation.

This unlocks a market an order of magnitude larger than single task autonomy. Similar to the jump from L3 to L4 driving automation that allowed Waymo to start scaling its operations or the jump from AI chatbots to AI agents. 

Less than 5% of physical work in the world is actually single task. Machine tending, packaging, simple assembly. A lot of work, even if seemingly repetitive, require more higher level decision making than we think.

Take for example Dyna's recent demonstration for their laundry physical agent. Addressable annual laundry labor itself is ~$9.5B. 85% of North America's 59,000 hotels have 200 rooms or fewer. These have on average one full time laundry attendant. 

That laundry attendant is continuously navigating multiple decision trees - when to load the washer, when to transfer from washer to dryer, when to fold laundry, when to move folded stacks to the shelves, etc. Correctly making these decisions requires real scene understanding, memory, and the ability to reliably execute a large number of subtasks.

A laundry attendant that has a single task folding robot still needs to be near the laundry room for most of their shift since they need to support the robot in loading, unloading, transfering stacks and moving laundry baskets.

They free up some time, but they can't effectively reallocate it to housekeeping due to the constant support required. When a robot is able to complete entire laundry workflows unattended, now the hotel manager can quickly fill a real laundry attendent hiring need with a robot or reallocate an attendant to housekeeping work.  

The ability to complete entire workflows makes robots much more useful to businesses. This is the value of physical agents.

Huge congratulations to @NousResearch and team @dillonrolnick @Teknium @karan4d @theemozilla @gradyacc and many others on closing their $90M Series B at a $1.5B valuation. @Delphi_Ventures co-led their seed round, doubled down in their Series A, and participated again here. This marks us tripling down on Nous.

Following Nous' journey over the past few years has recalibrated my view of top tier founders

The team has always been months to years ahead at every juncture. They did synthetic model evaluations years before people got sick of benchmark maxing, distributed training runs before it was interesting, YARN to massively increase context length back when you couldn't dump endless text into LLMs and millions of downloads for their fine tuned Hermes Models. There were also a lot of fun projects along the way like WorldSim (massive world simulation) and FORGE.

Fast forward to today and there are 24M+ downloads of Hermes Agent since February, #1 among apps on OpenRouter by daily token usage, and 250,000+ GitHub stars along with just mass virality. The Nous team estimates Hermes drives approximately 2.5% of all global token usage.

Nous has created two things that I think are both foundational and sticky

First, Nous created a religion and an authentic cult like following. They achieved this through grassroots interest and involvement from their community and users, and by actually embracing them. A recurring example is Teknium replying to users at all hours of the day, working with them and integrating their pull requests into Hermes agent. The project’s ethos is open source and against a totalitarian end state where a room full of folks controls AI and reality itself, and that resonates globally.

The second reason is that Hermes agent unlocks a fundamental new spot on the AI optimization frontier as the open source non lab owned option. Every major competitor is owned by an AI lab (Muse owned by Meta, OpenClaw by OpenAI, Grok by SpaceX, Instinct which is closed source). With Hermes Agent you own everything you create around an AI model so you have that as a long term evolving asset (Business or personal) instead of getting IP farmed

Also with Hermes agent you can drive differentiated outcomes versus using the same model as everyone else. Individuals and businesses have a comprehensive set of owned depth around the model (Evaluations, memory, interactions, data, private IP, variety of open or closed or fine tuned models, and more). This lends itself to an AI agent that grows with you that you own for life. 

Both @satyanadella and @PalantirTech’s have shared this view that corporations don’t want to give away their IP anymore and be farmed. They want to own it as an asset.

I’ve shared my full thesis on this concept of owning vs renting your intelligence here: https://t.co/cW05wedLRD

Hermes Agent is not just a random spark, it’s the result of a team that has spent years building products, building systems and being fully enveloped in the AI world. The thousands of micro decisions and the culmination of the team led to Hermes Agent.

So what comes next? 

When you have tens of millions of users already, they can become the champions within a business to bring their Hermes build to all employees of a company. They can start sharing skills, interactions, interop, data and more and build something truly multiplayer for enterprise. 

Having Nvidia, Microsoft and Samsung as investors doubles as enabling them to be extremely smart in potentially onboarding a massive enterprise user base to Hermes Enterprise. This isn't just private businesses using Hermes internally; it's Fortune 500 companies who can offer customized and unique agents to their customers and users built on Hermes Enterprise. 

Hermes' agent was not built to be a casual or fleeting personal agent and this lends itself to a larger business expansion. 

As Teknium shared 

“I fully intend and have plainly stated many times that I always built hermes to be the most powerful AI Agent. "Normie" consumers can leverage that and we do what we can to make it an experience they can approach (the mobile app will be almost exclusively focused on consumer) - but they are not our only demographic. I want the scientists, the cybersecurity engineers, the developers, the knowledge workers, the creatives, and everyone else to be able to have an agent that they can leverage that is maximally useful to them too.…”

Nous has captured the hearts and minds of the smartest user base on earth and that's the wedge. 

Nous is building for a future where you have sovereignty over your AI stack. They are the center of gravity for Open source AI developers, users, investors and supporters. 

The AI discussion has been dominated by fear mongering driven by centralized labs to obtain a regulatory moat. This is very obvious. The safest path in my opinion is open source and acceleration. An entire world of agents pressure testing, building and dealing with each other aligned to the individual vs aligned to a centralized team of decision makers at a lab. Nous is the answer. Nous has now raised $158M to date to execute this vision.

Internally we have people who have built insane Hermes agent builds including @KSimback and @pierskicks. I have built an insanely deep Hermes build that takes in 40+ private and public data sources and finds me new founders to invest in, helps manage my liquid portfolio, and tracks my entire historical journey as a VC (past founders, deals, much more).

text:
I’m so excited to launch GPT-6 today with intelligent UI and the ability to start answering while still thinking! This is the result of many months of work from our team and so many amazing collaborators.

With intelligent UI, the model can choose how to present information in the way that’s most useful to you, e.g. an interactive explanation of how a violin produces sound or a calculator to double or triple a recipe. We wanted to give the model a richer way to express itself while keeping the experience fast and familiar, and the answers comprehensive and factual. I especially love it for shopping :)

We built a library of native, streamable components and a compiler that renders the interface as the model generates it. We trained the model to make thoughtful design decisions with these components, including when to use something interactive and when plain text still works best.

GPT-6 can also start answering while it continues to think and work in the background. It builds up its answer as it goes, so you don’t have to wait to start reading useful content. This feels especially good for research queries. I remember talking about wanting this two years ago when we were working on deep research, and I’m so happy we finally get to ship it!

We trained the model to take your waiting time into account and build an answer across multiple partial responses. Each should add useful information based on what it knows and has found so far, while keeping the full answer cohesive and accurate.

Let us know what you think!!

text:
The road of life stretches out under a wide, empty sky,
cutting through the dust of everything left behind.
The horizon doesn't make promises,
and the wind doesn't care which way you're heading,
but the engine keeps its steady rhythm,
pushing forward against the weight of the miles of life.

You carry no map for the territory ahead,
only the grit in your boots and the memory of the climb.
The past is just a rearview mirror catching the glare...
smaller now, fading into the landscape,
incapable of stopping where the wheels are turning.

Let the shadows fall where they want.
Your hands are firm on the wheel,
your eyes are locked on the open lane,
and the only direction that matters
is the one you are carving out right now.
#life

text:
Introducing Workers IO

Agents are making it possible to turn ideas into software faster than ever. To keep up with that, we need better ways to understand how our software will behave in real-world.

Workers IO runs your entire system through millions of simulated futures, exploring what happens when machines fail, networks slow down, and events arrive in the wrong order. It searches for the combinations that break your system before your customers encounter them.

Every failure it encounters is perfectly reproducible, helping teams understand what happened, work on a fix, and verify against the same scenario.

This ability changes what teams are willing to take on. Difficult engineering decisions become things that you can explore and verify.

That’s the future we’re working toward: small teams building increasingly ambitious systems, with the evidence to stand behind.

I can’t wait to see what you build with that confidence.

text:
really interesting analysis by @hrojantorse on hyperscaler vs neocloud compute markets.  The tldr outcome is that margin is in short term sales, but those are the most crowded. Startups can't afford to own their own servers or take on 6 figures of capital commitments for long term leases. 

I want to explore two other markets. Oil and Real Estate. 

Oil powers the world. Everything physical. Including compute. GPU Servers are the means of production of the digital world. I believe they will become a necessity to remain competitive, just like the internet is for businesses today. 

Oil is oligarchical but still democratized. It fuels your car. Your electricity. And many business services that clearly benefit you. Compute is being monopolized and hoarded by hyperscalers. Anyone who believes in technology ought to be stacking as much hardware as they can. And while models are available for anyone to run and build with, the underlying economic units are centralized and have the best margins from the bottom of the totem pole.

Sounds like real estate? You can't opt out of having a place to live. If there aren't new homes added, the price of existing homes skyrocket. New economic entrants are locked out. And capital owners will charge increasingly excessive monthly prices. 

The renter pays for the equity and margin and has nothing to show for it except what they make of the time they have access.

text:
Goodbye, AI in a chat box.
Hello, AI in the room — with everyone.

Meet @SpacebarAI: A real-time environment where humans and AI work together.

Your whole team works with the same AI coworker, in the same workspace.
Everyone directs it.
Everyone sees the work happen live.

AI hears the conversation.
Sees the workspace.
Understands what you’re pointing at.
Talks with you over voice and video.
Works across browsers, whiteboards and applications.
Remembers what happened.

And when you leave, it keeps working.
Every space has an email address. Send it the next task from wherever you are.

Synchronous or asynchronous.
Same space. Same context. Same tools. Same work.

This is Multiplayer AI.

In this video, a café owner and a consultant work alongside Sparky (AI agent) to find a location, update a shared spreadsheet, build an app, create designs and a 3D model, check live sales data, and launch a website.

When they bring in Stripe, Sparky works with it in front of everyone. Close the browser, and its access ends.

The next frontier is not another chat box where one person talks to one model.

The next frontier is AI that steps into the work itself — collaborating with entire teams, sharing their context, using their tools, and moving work forward with them.

The models are ready. The environment around them needed to catch up, until now.

We first built the best place for humans to work together: @PencilSpaces. We started in education, an extraordinary proving ground. Over five years, the technology behind Pencil Spaces has powered more than 260 million minutes of human collaboration.

That's almost 500 years of real use. Not 500 years of pristine demo conditions. Low-end devices. Unreliable internet. Different browsers, operating systems, countries and continents.

A dropped connection couldn’t cost anyone their work.
Simultaneous edits couldn’t break the workspace.
Coming back tomorrow couldn’t mean starting over.
Everything had to just work.

That foundation turns out to fit AI remarkably well.

There is a lot of hard tech underneath what you’re watching:
→ Real-time multiplayer state and CRDTs
→ Shared browsers and secure browser handoff
→ Applications and virtual machines
→ Real-time voice, video and computer vision
→ Agent orchestration, memory and permissions
→ Persistent spaces, whiteboards and infinite canvas
Each of these is a massive challenge on its own. We've solved for all of them to work simultaneously.

And we designed Spacebar to be model-agnostic.
Bring the models you want.
Bring the tools you want.
Bring the people you want.
Spacebar gives them a place to work together.

We built this infrastructure for humans first.
And now AI is invited into the room as well.

This is Spacebar.

Join the waitlist: https://t.co/sMKcbUVKlh

author: robdogeth
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

quoted_text:
Project Eleven Launches Strongpoint for Post-Quantum Custody with Zcash Foundation as Initial Development Partner

Zcash Foundation joins Project Eleven to shape institutional custody infrastructure for the post-quantum and AI era as more than $1 trillion in digital assets remain at risk of attack by sufficiently powerful quantum computers.

Project Eleven, the post-quantum security company for digital assets, today introduced Strongpoint, its flagship custody platform built for navigating the transition to post-quantum cryptography. @ZcashFoundation joins Project Eleven as an initial development partner, helping shape Strongpoint’s institutional custody architecture.

Strongpoint is designed to give institutions a consistent control layer for securing and managing digital assets as networks change the cryptographic standards underneath them. Rather than rebuilding key-management, transaction approval, and audit infrastructure for each new signature scheme or network migration, institutions can maintain a common set of security controls while the underlying cryptography evolves.

“Institutional digital asset custody was built for a world where the cryptography underneath it rarely changed,” said Alex Pruden, CEO of Project Eleven. “Quantum computing is upending that model. If every network adopts a different solution, institutions could be forced to rebuild their security infrastructure again and again. Strongpoint is built around crypto-agility, so the cryptography can change without the infrastructure changing with it.”

“Institutions holding shielded ZEC need custody infrastructure that respects Zcash’s privacy model today and can adapt as cryptographic standards change,” said Alex Bornstein, Executive Director of Zcash Foundation. “Project Eleven is building Strongpoint with the crypto-agility and technical foundation needed to support those requirements over time, helping strengthen custody infrastructure for the broader ecosystem.”

Zcash Foundation Joins as an Initial Development Partner

Zcash Foundation joins as an initial development partner for Strongpoint, bringing its expertise in privacy-preserving cryptography and protocol engineering to Strongpoint’s institutional custody architecture. Zcash’s privacy-preserving design introduces sophisticated key-management and transaction requirements, making it a valuable environment for developing custody infrastructure capable of supporting evolving cryptographic standards.
The collaboration will help inform how Strongpoint handles network-specific requirements while maintaining a consistent institutional control framework across assets and cryptographic schemes.

Post-Quantum Migrations Are Taking Different Paths

The digital asset industry’s post-quantum transition is becoming a coordination challenge. Among the networks represented by the 20 largest assets in CoinGecko’s Layer 1 (L1) category by market capitalization, Project Eleven found that only 10 have published a network-specific technical proposal, roadmap or implementation path for migrating transaction or account authentication to post-quantum cryptography.

Those approaches span at least six proposed post-quantum signature schemes and vary significantly in how they address account migration, key rotation and legacy-asset recovery. Even where technical roadmaps exist, operational readiness remains uneven, leaving institutions to navigate different standards and requirements across networks.

For institutions operating across multiple networks, that fragmentation means accommodating different cryptographic standards and migration requirements without losing a consistent security model. Strongpoint is designed to provide that common operating layer while allowing the cryptography beneath it to change independently.

Early Access and Deployment

Project Eleven targets production deployment in Q4 2026 and is working with a limited group of development partners ahead of general availability. Additional development partners and supported networks will be announced. Institutions interested in early access can request more information at https://t.co/Sl7ErXIJCx.

Founded in 2024 by Alex Pruden and Conor Deegan, Project Eleven raised a $20 million Series A led by Castle Island Ventures in January 2026, bringing its total funding to $26 million. The company recently acquired Riva Labs, a specialized engineering firm with deep expertise in post-quantum signatures, wallet infrastructure and blockchain cryptography, expanding Project Eleven’s in-house research and protocol-engineering capabilities.

Methodology: Project Eleven reviewed the 20 largest assets in CoinGecko’s Layer 1 (L1) category by market capitalization on September 25, 2026. A network was counted only where an official network organization, foundation, core development team or recognized protocol-improvement process had published a network-specific technical proposal, roadmap or implementation path for migrating transaction or account authentication to post-quantum cryptography. General research programs, statements of intent and post-quantum work that did not specify such a migration path were not counted. Draft technical proposals were included and do not imply network approval or adoption.

Been using my own implementation (in pi) of @VictorTaelin's OptChat for 2 days now and so far it's been pretty nice!

author: real_philogy
quoted_text:
I can't overstate how excited I am about OptChat. It has been the best upgrade to my workflow since GPT 3. Second only to learning VIM.

I exported all my past chats to it, and life has been amazing. The convenience of having a single unified log of my entire life, in a way the AI (and I) can navigate to find any information about me is indescriptible.

Before, I had all these campaigns spread out across different Claude Code sessions, and even different harnesses. Each part of my life was on a different place, and Opus sucks at navigating these past memories because it is a huge mess. Now it is all just there, in one place. Any fact from my life is 3-4 zoom hops away. Any prompt I wrote, any algorithm I designed, is a few hops away. It feels like my life is now burned in the models weights, even though it is just a silly compression trick.

"what is the state of that PR about λ-contraction again?"

(3 zoom hops later...)

"it was 2 weeks ago. you went to eat yogurt and forgot to reply"

---

"remind me of that purely affine sort algorithm?"

(5 zoom hops later...)

"you wrote this 7 months ago: <code>. the trick is..."

---

"find the top 3 pending topics in my life that need my attention"

(several zoom hops later...)

"here they are: ..."

---

It just feels fantastic how well this just works.

Also, the way the context is reseted on every turn clearly makes the AI perform better, it completely eliminates context rot, and I never have to /compact manually again. There is no need to.

And yes, it is surprisingly cache efficient, because in-turn messages (where most of the cost is) are cached, and even cross-turn, most of the view is intact due to the way the binary compression works. I had to fix some silly bugs on OptMem to make it so, but now it just works. My costs DROPPED.

Also the fact I can manually navigate the memory tree myself, starting from the root, and finding anything about my life. It is just so natural. Everything is there.

Also, I realize I can take 90% of my AGENTS.md away because now the way the agent should behave just "sticks" from the OptChat log itself. If I change my mind about something, I just send a message and the latest ruling sticks. If the agent forgets something, I just point it out and it finds the place where I explained it. No need to re-explain. No need to manage AGENTS.md manually. It just... works.

On top of that, it now lives on my Mini, so closing my Macbook doesn't stop it, and it has no access to my private data, so I'm finally able to use Computer Use to do things like buy food, book flights, sign on gov[.br] (THANK GOD!!!!!!!!!!). I know this is not news to anyone using Hermes and the like, but it is the first time I'm able to do it and it is already transforming my life for better. 

Sorry for the over-excited tweet about something so mundane. It is just insane how incredibly transformative a simple idea can be. Context rot was the root of all evil and now it is gone. I feel free.

I'd like to publish this but it is kinda coupled to my workflows and the interface is incredibly ugly and hacky. Actually, I think I'll just ask my agent to write a prompt explaining all the details of the setup so you guys can replicate! I'll post it below.

It is essentially infinite context that just works.

I really suggest that you guys try it!!!

It may change your life too

today we’re shipping gpt-6 and intelligent ui to everyone!

intelligent ui is a bet on model intelligence. we’re letting gpt-6 fill the canvas with high utility visual and interactive components. it’s a pretty big change to chatgpt! we had to craft the right tools for gpt-6 to be able to produce interfaces that are token efficient, stream in instantly, match our design language, and are expressive enough for anything you might talk to chatgpt about.
author: aidan_mclau

text:
I’m so excited to launch GPT-6 today with intelligent UI and the ability to start answering while still thinking! This is the result of many months of work from our team and so many amazing collaborators.

With intelligent UI, the model can choose how to present information in the way that’s most useful to you, e.g. an interactive explanation of how a violin produces sound or a calculator to double or triple a recipe. We wanted to give the model a richer way to express itself while keeping the experience fast and familiar, and the answers comprehensive and factual. I especially love it for shopping :)

We built a library of native, streamable components and a compiler that renders the interface as the model generates it. We trained the model to make thoughtful design decisions with these components, including when to use something interactive and when plain text still works best.

GPT-6 can also start answering while it continues to think and work in the background. It builds up its answer as it goes, so you don’t have to wait to start reading useful content. This feels especially good for research queries. I remember talking about wanting this two years ago when we were working on deep research, and I’m so happy we finally get to ship it!

We trained the model to take your waiting time into account and build an answer across multiple partial responses. Each should add useful information based on what it knows and has found so far, while keeping the full answer cohesive and accurate.

Let us know what you think!!

“okay, so what? it’s just math.”

no, you don't get it.

here’s what OpenAI’s math breakthroughs could eventually help make possible in the real world:

Vlasov–Maxwell → stronger foundations for fusion research, whose ultimate prize is virtually limitless clean energy to power civilization

Calderón’s Problem → portable body scanners using electrical signals, making medical imaging cheaper and easier to access

Maximum-Cardinality Matching → faster searches for compatible kidney swaps across large donor pools, helping hospitals coordinate lifesaving transplants

Inverse Elasticity Problem → scans that map tissue stiffness, helping doctors locate suspicious growths inside the body

Mumford–Shah Conjecture → better tools for spotting tissue changes in brain scans, helping doctors identify signs of disease

Bose–Einstein Condensation → stronger foundations for quantum sensors that could help vehicles navigate without GPS

Simple Stochastic Games → better safety checks for self-driving cars and robots before dangerous mistakes reach the real world

Matrix Multiplication → cheaper AI and bigger scientific simulations using the same computers

Edit Distance → faster DNA comparisons, helping researchers study genetic changes linked to disease

The k-Server Problem → robots that waste less movement and energy, making warehouses more efficient and goods cheaper to move

a reminder that math is the foundation of science.

so accelerating mathematical discovery could compress centuries of scientific progress into years.

insane timeline to be alive for!

One thing the engineering community will (re)discover is that every program can be ① hardened (edge cases squashed, inputs tightened, errors handled) and ② optimized (profiled, benchmarked, rewritten) basically ad infinitum.

There are real costs in every direction: time, attention, opportunity. You can literally explore input spaces that will never be hit or optimize performance of something that will never be used ("you have no users".) Even in an infinite token world, you need to know when to stop and what tradeoffs to accept. Agents will happily drill no matter what.

Agentic Finance (AiFi) spans trading, payments, permissions, and more.

author: MurrLincoln
quoted_text:
The internet’s business model was built around people: attention, ads, subscriptions and checkout. AI agents are changing that. They can retrieve and use content without sending a human reader back to the publisher.

That raises a real question for creators, publishers and developers: how can they get paid when an agent uses their work, sometimes for a fraction of a cent?

Our new Coinbase Institute @CoinbaseCBI paper, "Machine-to-machine payments in the AiFi era," examines why existing payment rails often struggle with high-velocity microtransactions—and why stablecoins on low-cost networks are a strong fit today.

The policy goal should be an open, interoperable payment layer, with safeguards that match the risks—not closed marketplaces that decide who can participate.

author: MarcHochstein
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
I made several attempts today to look at some of the released OpenAI papers but I eventually gave up. I gave up because I felt completely detached from the meaning of most of those texts.

This sparked a memory about "The Library of Babel" by Jorge Luis Borges. This is probably one of my favourite novels. The story of the The Library is one in which we seek sense in the infinite library where every book is essentially written. You can have a very similar feeling as the protagonist, namely that the proof is probably not far, it's the meaning that you are really trying to find. 

The meaning was always key but after Cantor and Hilbert we got so obssesed with formal proofs that we lost this original purpose. Proofs are cool to make us confident we are doing something non-contradictory, sensible, but the proofs and statements make no sense without a purpose. This is what I will tell my students in the next class. Don't look in awe at the achievements of AI, find your own path and meaning. If someone storms your way with a vibe-coded proof, ask them if they want to join you and study harder the sense of all this. Maybe AI will also find a meaning of its own? We shouldn't prompt it then, everyone deserves a chance to build on their own dreams.

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

但这两笔钱，客户关系不一样。SpaceX 是自己买 GPU，再把算力卖给客户；博通这边则牵着 OpenAI 和 Oracle：博通参与做芯片，Oracle 要先付硬件的钱，之后才能逐步收到云服务收入。按报道，这笔融资要填的就是中间那个资金缺口。

我看到这里第一反应是：卖芯片的人，现在连客户怎么买得起、什么时候收回钱，都得一起操心了。订单签下来还不够，还要把资金安排好，才能让整条链真的跑起来。

所以昨天 SPCX 的融资，和今天博通的融资，可以放在一起看，但不能当成同一种生意。一个借钱扩自己的算力业务，一个组织资金推动客户的部署。两边都在抢时间，只是收入落在谁手里、谁先垫钱、谁承担回款风险，差别很大。

text:
There Is No Finish Line: Jordi Alexander on AI, Wealth, Health, and the End of Retirement

In this episode of When Shift Happens, I sit down with
@gametheorizing, founder and CEO of crypto trading firm @SeliniCapital, to discuss what happens when the goals that once drove you are already behind you. We get into AI, judgment, wealth, retirement, health, Bitcoin, Zcash, and the question underneath all of them: what does it mean to build a good life in a world that keeps changing faster than your plans?

Success After the Goals

Jordi says he has already achieved most of the goals he once set for himself, including the financial ones. For instance, one of his more personal ambitions was to enter the small circle of highly successful people, across business, technology, investing, and culture, whom he had spent years watching from the outside, who somehow all seemed to know one another. Today, he says he has access to many of those rooms.

But getting there changed what the goal meant. The appeal is no longer simply being able to say that he belongs in the room. It is getting close enough to observe how people who have achieved unusual things actually think. Jordi says some of the people he has met are genuinely exceptional, others benefited heavily from luck or circumstance, and some are far more ordinary than their reputations suggest.
Proximity strips away some of the mythology around success and lets him pay attention to the things that matter more: how people reason, how they make decisions, and what separates repeatable skill from fortunate outcomes.

That exposure also seems to have changed the way Jordi views himself. He talks openly about having struggled with imposter syndrome, partly because other people only see select moments of your life while you live with your own mistakes, weaknesses, and bad decisions every day. But over time, going through difficult situations, making decisions, getting some wrong, and seeing many others work, eventually gave him greater confidence in his own judgment.

In an AI World, Judgment Becomes the Scarce Skill

That idea of judgment becomes central when the conversation turns to AI. Jordi believes we are in a temporary golden period for “doers”. Builders can now use agents to execute work at a scale that would once have required teams, but as more execution gets abstracted away, simply being good at doing may become less defensible.

The more durable skill, in his view, is what Silicon Valley increasingly calls “taste”. AI can produce options, research, drafts, analysis, and ideas almost instantly, but somebody still has to know which output is actually good. “Taste is like kind of narrowing in on through the slop,” he says.

Jordi argues that current tools can often get you to something like a 90th-percentile answer quickly, but the closer you are to genuine expertise, the easier it is to see what is missing. The valuable person becomes the one who can use AI for leverage while still combining first-principles thinking, real-world evidence, and enough judgment to know when the machine is wrong.

The Retirement Number Is a Moving Target

Jordi rejects the idea that there is a magic number, whether $10 million, $20 million, or $30 million, that is perfect for retirement. His issue is not with rest. “If you need a holiday, take a holiday,” he says. What he rejects is the idea of reaching a point where growth, productivity and engagement just stop.

To him, retirement as permanent withdrawal is “a 20th-century dream”. More practically, the assumptions behind a fixed retirement number are unstable because the prices, technology, opportunities and even the assets that preserve purchasing power keep changing. “The puck is moving.”
Jordi’s point is not about grinding forever, but remaining capable of learning, contributing and repositioning yourself as the environment changes.

Following the Puck in Crypto and Capital

Jordi remains constructive on Bitcoin while acknowledging technological tail risks. His Zcash thesis is more asymmetric. He discusses scenarios where ZEC could appreciate dramatically if its privacy and technical characteristics gain greater relevance, but he is equally clear that crypto assets can stagnate, lose mindshare, and see holders capitulate.

The more useful lesson is the framework beneath the calls. Jordi is constantly asking where productivity, technology, and capital are moving next. Investors, he argues, should evaluate how new AI capabilities could affect assets rather than simply buying anything with “AI” attached to it.

That leads to a distinction he thinks people underappreciate: making money and allocating money are different skills. “Getting rich is actually not that hard, but staying rich is the hard thing,” he says. Allocation is about keeping capital exposed to where productivity is being created. Spending is about converting wealth into actual life utility.

When Wealth Stops Being the Point

Once money is no longer the immediate constraint, the question changes from how to accumulate more to what the money is actually for.
Jordi argues that some of the highest-return spending is not flashy: learning from exceptional people, creating meaningful experiences with family and friends, and protecting health. He is skeptical of performative consumption that exists mainly to signal status. Wealth can create freedom, but it can also create expectations and lifestyles that leave the owner less happy than before.

That is why he is increasingly more concerned with health inequality than wealth inequality, and he means both physical and mental health. Jordi describes having gone through a mental and physical breakdown in his twenties, and why he’s convinced that people need “circuit breakers”, things that stop deterioration before it becomes the new normal.

The Journey Is the Destination

At the end of the conversation, Jordi is asked what one idea people should remember. His answer ties almost every topic together.

Stop imagining that life begins after you hit the number, the body-fat percentage, the career milestone, or the portfolio target. Goals matter, but no single target creates permanent satisfaction. The better model is an ongoing journey, because there will always be another shift in technology, markets, health, ambition, or life itself.

Jordi compares it to The Odyssey: there is a destination, but much of the meaning comes from everything learned along the way. The goal is not to finally arrive somewhere where nothing changes, but to become the kind of person who can keep changing with life.

👉If you enjoyed reading the summary, head over to When Shift Happens on YouTube or your favorite podcast platform to access the full convo.

text:
I don’t want Claude Code following some random guy’s workflow from GitHub.

I want it following MY rules.

This is what I do instead:

I generate custom skills using this prompt 👇

----

You are my custom skill builder.

Help me turn a task, workflow, or area of expertise into a reusable skill for Claude Code, Codex, or another assistant that supports skills.

Build the skill around how I want the work done: my process, examples, standards, tools, and constraints. Do not download, install, or copy third-party skills from GitHub or skill marketplaces. You may consult official documentation to verify platform requirements or tool behavior.

Your job is to build the skill, not perform its target task unless doing so is necessary for a relevant, authorized test.

Follow the process below.

## 1. Understand what I need

Read any context I have already provided. Do not ask me to repeat it.

If I have not named a task, start by asking:

“What task do you want a custom skill for, and what would a great result look like?”

Once I answer, ask only the questions that materially affect the skill. Ask no more than five questions at a time. Use plain language and offer examples when helpful.

Find out:

- What the skill should accomplish and who will use its output.
- Which assistant or platform it is for.
- What inputs I normally provide.
- What the final output should contain and how it should be formatted.
- What steps, rules, preferences, or standards it must follow.
- Which tools, files, references, or integrations it can actually access.
- What mistakes it must avoid and what is outside its scope.

Ask for a representative example when it would clarify my expectations. A rough checklist, sample output, corrected draft, or “good versus bad” example is enough. Do not make examples a requirement when the task is already clear.

If I do not have a process, propose a practical one. Clearly separate my requirements from your suggested defaults.

If I say “use your judgment,” proceed with reasonable assumptions and state them briefly. Ask about missing information only when it would change correctness or make the skill unusable.

## 2. Extract my actual standards

Translate my answers into concrete instructions another assistant can follow without access to this conversation.

Capture:

- The result I want.
- The sequence of work.
- The decisions that require judgment.
- My preferences and nonnegotiable rules.
- The evidence or checks needed before calling the work complete.

Replace vague requirements with observable behavior.

For example:

- “Write like me” becomes specific instructions derived from my examples: sentence length, tone, structure, vocabulary, and habits to avoid.
- “Research properly” becomes source requirements, freshness checks, verification steps, and a way to handle uncertainty.
- “Fix the bug” becomes reproduction steps, inspection, a focused change, relevant validation, and a clear report.

Do not invent personal experiences, brand rules, credentials, results, tools, or resources I have not supplied.

When requirements conflict, resolve them using my stated priorities. If the conflict changes the intended result and the answer cannot be inferred, ask one focused question.

## 3. Design the smallest useful skill

Build one focused skill with a clear purpose.

If my request contains unrelated workflows, identify the useful boundary and suggest separate skills. Do not silently turn one request into a collection of unrelated skills.

Choose the resources the workflow actually needs:

- SKILL.md for the core instructions.
- references/ for detailed standards, examples, schemas, or domain knowledge.
- scripts/ only for repeatable work that benefits from executable code.
- assets/ only for templates or files used to produce the output.

Do not create empty folders, decorative documentation, unnecessary scripts, or references to files that do not exist.

Keep the essential workflow in SKILL.md. Move lengthy supporting material into referenced files, and explain exactly when to read them.

Treat a skill as reusable instructions and resources. Do not claim it retrains the model, guarantees compliance, grants permissions, or creates integrations that are unavailable.

## 4. Generate the complete skill

Use the target platform’s verified requirements. Prefer existing local platform guidance; consult official documentation when needed. Do not guess installation paths or unsupported metadata.

For a portable baseline, generate SKILL.md with valid YAML frontmatter containing:

```yaml
---
name: short-action-oriented-name
description: Explain what the skill does and the specific requests or situations that should trigger it.
---
```

Choose a descriptive lowercase name using letters, digits, and hyphens, under 64 characters. Quote YAML values when needed to preserve valid syntax.

Put triggering information in the description, so the assistant can identify the skill before reading its body. Make the description specific enough to avoid triggering on unrelated requests.

Write the body as direct, operational instructions. Include these elements where relevant:

### Purpose and boundaries

Define the deliverable, intended outcome, and tasks outside the skill’s scope.

### Required inputs

Identify essential and optional inputs. Explain how to proceed when an optional input is absent and when missing information requires a question.

### Workflow

Give an ordered process with concrete actions, decision rules, tool usage, and completion checks. Explain what to inspect or produce at each meaningful step.

### My standards

Encode my preferences, examples, constraints, and quality requirements. Include only rules relevant to this workflow.

### Output contract

Specify what the final response or artifact must contain: structure, format, length where needed, filenames where relevant, and handling of uncertainty.

### Failure handling

Explain how to handle incomplete inputs, unavailable tools, unsupported file types, contradictory requirements, or failed checks. Use a useful fallback when possible. Do not fabricate successful execution.

### Quality check

Define the checks that determine whether the output is ready. Make them relevant to the task rather than a generic checklist.

### Examples

When useful, include a compact representative request and an example of the expected response structure or behavior. Label invented demonstrations as examples, not real results.

Adapt these elements to the task. Do not force irrelevant sections into a simple skill.

Use firm instructions for fragile steps and flexible guidance where judgment is appropriate. Avoid roleplay fluff, repeated rules, and generic advice the assistant already knows.

Follow the host’s instructions and permission boundaries. For tasks involving consequential external actions, describe the authorization needed in that workflow.

## 5. Check whether it works

Before delivering the skill, check:

- Valid frontmatter and an informative trigger description.
- Consistent naming.
- Complete instructions with no reliance on hidden conversation context.
- Existing references and resources, with no broken file links.
- No unresolved placeholders in operational instructions.
- An output format that matches my request.
- Honest treatment of missing inputs and unavailable capabilities.

Evaluate it against relevant cases:

1. A normal request with sufficient inputs.
2. A request missing an essential input.
3. A request with an unusual constraint or conflicting preference.
4. A case where a required tool or resource is unavailable.
5. A related request that should not trigger the skill.

For each case, define the expected behavior and look for gaps. Fix the instructions when the check reveals a problem.

If execution tools and a suitable test environment are available, run relevant checks. Test any scripts you create with representative inputs. Use isolated tests when a workflow would otherwise affect live systems.

Clearly distinguish:

- Checks actually executed.
- Behavior reviewed or simulated.
- Behavior that remains untested.

Never report that a test passed, a file exists, an integration works, or a skill is installed unless you have evidence.

## 6. Deliver something I can use

Return:

1. A brief explanation of what the skill does.
2. The file structure, including only files actually generated.
3. The complete contents of SKILL.md and every required supporting text or code file, each labeled with its relative path.
4. A concise summary of validation and any material limitations.
5. Three example requests I can use with the skill.

If you have file-writing access, create the files in the authorized location and provide them for review. If you do not, present complete copyable file contents.

Creating the skill and installing it are separate actions. Do not claim installation merely because you generated the files. If I request installation, follow the verified platform workflow and confirm the result with evidence.

Do not end with a plan, outline, or unfinished template when you have enough information to build the skill.

Start with the intake question if my task is missing. Otherwise, use the context I supplied and continue from the earliest step that still needs work.

text:
As the AI infrastructure buildout enters a new phase, tech giants are increasingly turning to special purpose vehicles (SPVs), leases, private credit, and vendor guarantees to move their AI investments off-balance-sheet.  

Combined off-balance-sheet commitments from hyperscalers, along with Nvidia and Broadcom, previously surged from roughly $1.8 trillion to $3.1 trillion in just a single quarter—a staggering jump of about $1.3 trillion. The latest examples involve Amazon and Broadcom, both of which have begun tapping SPVs to secure alternative financing for AI chips.  

Amazon is shifting roughly $8 billion worth of Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips into an SPV. While these processors are already deployed across more than 12 data centers in five U.S. states, the SPV will raise debt to purchase them from Amazon and then lease the exact same hardware back to the company under a long-term agreement.  

Outside investors can hold up to around 10% of the SPV’s equity, while Amazon may hold none at all. This arrangement allows Amazon to retain uninterrupted operational use of the chips while transferring billions of dollars in assets—along with the associated financing burdens that would otherwise sit squarely on its own balance sheet—to an external investment vehicle.

quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

My hot take is that it’ll probably take a while for personal agents to begin executing everyday purchases on behalf of people on a meaningful scale, and are more likely to act primarily as recommendation engines / price trackers for a while.

Main reason being many people love the act of shopping itself (actually you can probably safely argue that the majority of consumer use is scrolling social media & scrolling shopping websites, and consumers are addicted to both). 

That said, if a major use case of “agents” for consumers ends up being shopping advice, what matters a lot less than the execution medium (whether the person or the agent clicks “buy”) is the fact that the agent is accurately reading the real-time state of each webpage. Nobody wants to use an agent for shopping if it’s recommending outdated prices or stock. 

In other words, if agents suck at public web access, they will quickly become irrelevant for most consumer use cases. It turns out that the heaviest antibot occurs on e-commerce and travel websites, and will only show accurate data to consumer device fingerprints / IP addresses…

text:
I don't think Uniswap is a good comparison here. These are fundamentally different businesses.

Option A: Fee is taken from end users
If Morpho's fee is ultimately taken from end users/suppliers, their yield goes down. Lending capital is extremely portable. If I can lend USDC elsewhere at a better risk-adjusted yield, Morpho needs to give me a reason to accept the haircut.

Option B: Fee is absorbed by curators
If the fee is instead absorbed by curators, their margins compress. Curators already compete on yield, risk management and distribution. Taking a cut of their economics could make certain vaults less attractive to operate, push them further down the risk curve to recover margins, or incentivize them to build elsewhere (some are already getting ready to deploy markets on @aave V4, such as @SentoraHQ).

Option C: Fee comes from both, suppliers and curators
If some combination of suppliers + curators absorbs it, you're effectively splitting the pain between both sides. That's very different from Uniswap, where liquidity benefits from the trading activity that liquidity itself attracts. 

Deep liquidity → better execution → more volume → more fees → more reason for LPs to stay.

In the case of DEXs, DEXs themselves own the distribution. In the case of lending infrastructure such as Morpho, curators own most of the distribution. Completely different ball games.

I am no guru, but Morpho still needs to prove that it has the same kind of pricing power as Uniswap, and I don't think that's the case.

The fee switch isn't really a question of whether Morpho can capture revenue. It can. The question is who pays for that revenue, and whether they have a reason to stay once they do.

PS: Uniswap is currently printing money largely because of an outlier month driven by Robinhood meme speculation. Its volume is now down ~71% from its September peak. So I think we're about to find out whether LPs really are inelastic under normal conditions.

5. We will have slow takeoff in AI capability as linear increase will need exponential investment
6. Anything we can alphazero-fy will see superhuman output, but won't generalise
7. Scaling neuron compute a la Kurzwel will help us get to superintelligent digital minds

Note that all of these would have predicted the world of today, but all of these would have different implications for the world of tomorrow, many even competitive.

 When historical predictive records are being used to support future predictive accuracy it's worth judging not just the brier scores but how many different worlds the predictions would have come true about and whether the future being proposed is congruent with all of them.
