text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

text:
This might be the biggest opportunity blockchains have ever had. 

Technology has mostly been built around durable yet centralized trust systems. But the factors acting against these systems are getting more powerful as we near Super Intelligence™️. 

Obviously code can break due to the sheer mathematical progress AI is bringing, but less obviously, humans can be broken too. Impersonation, blackmail, and other forms of social engineering attacks are only going to get more advanced. As such, just fixing holes in code made to secure our lives is not enough, to build truly trustworthy systems of value, you will have to decentralize them and add immutability such that no single actor can, in most clear words, “not fuck it up.” This is exactly what Ethereum was built for. 

“Alright man, so what is Ethereum doing to survive this age? Are we cooked?”

Quite the contrary, the frontier is moving fast, but Ethereum is moving faster. Some quick points: 

1. The Hegotá upgrade will set the tone. 

This upgrade will make Ethereum cryptographically agile. 

EIP-8141, lovingly known as “Frames,” changes Ethereum accounts at the root level so that transaction validations can be programmable instead of tied to the ECSDA key (the thing Justin is warning people about in his post). Essentially accounts can choose how to authenticate instead of being tied to the current status quo. There are a few quantum proof signatures out there like ML-DSA and SPHINCS, with frames you can choose whatever and also be open to even more gigabrain ones to come. When you are faced with a threat, agility is key, and Hegotá sets the tone for that agility.

2. The J* upgrade will produce a MVP quantum proof L1. 

Okay, I know what you’re thinking, “why would you ever name such a consequential thing ‘I*’???What is wrong with you??” Trust me I thought this too, but I was promptly educated that names are not finalized until we get closer, in fact, the names even get a fun emoji next to them (e.g The Hegotá upgrade emoji is a goat 🐐 IFYKYK :P)

ANYWAYS

Think of J* as answering “what are the minimal changes Ethereum needs to make if quantum computers exist tomorrow?”  

The goal here is to have enough to survive Q-day. Today, this maps to achieving a PQ heartbeat on consenus layers, leanDA PQ sampling, and leanSPHINCS transactions on execution. 

TLDR: the aim is to ship this and then play Alright by Kendrick shortly after: “we gon’ be alright!” 

4. The boxes are moving in real time 

If you’ve ever seen the strawmap (a proposed roadmap for Ethereum), you’ll know it has a lot of boxes. In particular, there is a quantum box. Also fun fact: it’s literally called a strawmap because it moves as research moves, and man is it moving! 

> On August 12, leanVM was moved forward from J* to I*
> A week later, the roadmap added the minimal viable post-quantum L1 milestone to J* 

If you’re ever wondering whether Ethereum is taking this seriously, just watch the boxes and see how they dance. 

5. AI is actually HELPING

AI makes cryptographic research faster, and AI assisted formal verification means you don’t have to trust AI’s answer. Check out some of @fradamt’s posts for more. 

6. Quantum is just one threat in a much bigger battle 

You can quantum proof a bank’s system but still be fallible to the humans that run it. Ethereum tackles this from both sides, it gardens the security while also distributing the authors of the network such that there is no single point of attack.

Other blockchains, and any place that stores value TBH, will begin to claim they are quantum proof, but they fail to address the threat of being human proof too. 

7. The grand prize is here, and Ethereum can grab it. 

A neutral and secure place for ALL value, that cannot be coerced by a government, a company, or Superintelligence. 

Your life, your story, your money, can be here, forever. And many generations from now, the kids will look up and think: thank god they tried. 

Godspeed. 

Ethereum.

quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

Anthropic 今天发布了 Claude Haiku 5.5。Haiku 是 Claude 家族里最小、最便宜的一档，排在 Sonnet 和 Opus 之下，主要用来跑量大、对成本敏感的任务。

这次最大的变化是价格。处理 10 万 Token 以内的请求，Haiku 5.5 每百万 Token 输入 0.1 美元、输出 0.5 美元，比 Haiku 4.5 便宜 90%。超过 10 万 Token 的长请求是 0.5 和 2.5 美元，便宜一半。上一代 Haiku 收到的请求里约 90% 都在 10 万 Token 以内，所以按官方估算，平均运行成本降了约 75%。

10 万 Token 大约是一本中篇小说的长度，客服对话、文档摘要、分类打标这类日常任务，基本都在这个范围里。

价格降了，能力也上来了。官方公布的测试里，操作电脑完成多步骤任务（OSWorld 2.1）的成绩从 Haiku 4.5 的 15.7% 涨到 72.4%；在命令行里自主完成编程任务（Terminal-Bench 4.0）从 0 涨到 39.2%。Anthropic 说它是目前速度最快的模型（Opus 开快速模式除外），Asana 实测任务完成延迟降低了 30% 以上。

官方推荐的用法有两类。一类是批量的重复活，比如摘要、分类、数据库查询，以及实时客服、浏览器自动操作这种要求响应快的场景。另一类是给大模型打下手：写代码时让 Opus 5.5 或 Sonnet 5.5 当主力，把零碎的子任务分给 Haiku 5.5 去做，也就是当子智能体。

Haiku 5.5 也是第一个能调节“投入力度”（effort）的 Haiku 模型，从低到最高分五档。简单任务开低档省钱，难的任务开高档换效果，开发者可以按任务选。

Haiku 5.5 今天起在 Claude API 以及亚马逊 AWS、谷歌云、微软 Azure 上可用，模型名 claude-haiku-5-5。

同时宣布的还有两件事。

Sonnet 5.5 读取缓存的价格减半，降到每百万 Token 0.1 美元。缓存就是把反复用到的内容（比如很长的系统提示词、整个代码库）存起来，下次直接读取，不用重新算。智能体任务里这部分开销占大头，官方估算这次降价让 Sonnet 5.5 跑大多数智能体任务便宜约 20%。

本周起，Max 和 Team 订阅用户每月会拿到一笔 API 额度：Max 5x 送 100 美元，Max 20x 送 200 美元，Team 最多 500 美元，团队成员共用。

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
I've read this post 5+ times and I increasingly have trouble with the core point.

If ECDSA breaks without warning, we have so much more to worry about than our magic internet money. Internet security as a whole is gone. SSL/TLS gone, the internet is now transparent.

Not just internet security as well - a large portion of physical security would become irrelevant too. You can't have secure digital locks if encryption is dead. You can't secure surveillance footage if the gateway it's stored on can be wiped out on a whim.

We would have much bigger problems than "your magic internet money gets stolen." The floor would drop out of the global economy.

Most importantly - the answer to transparent encryption simply cannot be "hide your magic internet money" when the internet wouldn't exist anymore. You'd be relying on this technology coming back online, and not just that, you'd be relying on the tokens you stashed away being the relevant ones when it does.

I get the ~reasonable dooming here, but if we're going to doom you have to take it to its conclusion. You're going to be much better off investing in gold or cylindrical lead if your core hypothesis is "ECDSA could be broken within months"

author: newmichwill
quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

OpenAI 722 篇数学论文威力真猛，极端情况下公钥直接能推出私钥。

以太坊核心研究员发出警告：币圈该进入防御模式了😲😲😲（必看、必做）

卧槽，OpenAI 这次公开的数学仓库，影响可能远远超出 AI 圈。

以太坊基金会核心研究员 Justin Drake 直接向整个加密行业发出警告：

保护比特币、以太坊等加密资产的椭圆曲线密码学，可能在量子计算机成熟之前，就被 AI 找到破解方法。

他甚至提出了一种极端情况：最快几个月内，攻击者可能只需要大型 GPU 集群运行一周，就能从公钥反推出私钥。

我们一直以为，只要助记词不泄露、硬件钱包不被攻破，资产就安全了。

但如果 AI 找到了破解底层密码算法的数学捷径，黑客可能根本不需要碰你的设备，只要拿到已经暴露的公钥，就有机会算出私钥。

交易所冷钱包、巨鲸地址、机构托管，以及大量依赖椭圆曲线签名的链上基础设施，都可能面临风险。

所以 Drake 呼吁整个行业开始准备进入钱包防御模式，说白了，就是大户和机构先把大部分资产有序转移到公钥尚未暴露的新地址，尽量减少旧公钥暴露带来的风险。

以后每次签名，也考虑更换地址。

他还点名 Binance、Robinhood、Bitfinex、Tether 等机构，呼吁提前加强防护。

不过，不同链和地址类型的保护机制并不相同，这套办法也无法替代真正的抗攻击密码学升级。

这一切的导火索，就是 OpenAI 公开的 722 篇数学手稿。

它让 Drake 开始认真考虑一个过去看起来很遥远的风险：

AI 可能突然发现人类几十年都没有找到的数学捷径，让原本需要天文数字计算量的密码学难题，变得可以被普通计算集群攻破。

不过目前没有证据证明 ECDSA 已被攻破，Drake 所说的几个月也只是极端风险推演，大家千万不要恐慌性转账。

但我觉得，所有加密圈的人都应该认真看待这次警告。

以前大家担心量子计算机会不会攻破比特币，现在连 AI 都成了必须考虑的潜在威胁。

加密行业可能需要提前为一场尚未发生的密码学危机做准备了。

text:
This founder built an AI voice agent that calls every new lead for his immigration law firm, in his own cloned voice. 

It qualifies them and books them with a lawyer. It saves his attorneys 4-to-5 hours a day...over $100,000 per year. 

He built it with a $10 phone number and a voice note from his iPhone.

So i asked him to show me live. He filled out his own website form, skipped the calendar, and his phone rang.

Here's @theachintsingh's actual system for an AI voice agent that follows up with every lead: 

Check out the full episode here: https://t.co/XG0pKr3Y3s

1) A lead fills out the form on his website, hosted on @Netlify. If they don't book a time, it goes to his master bot on Grok @Bot, then his follow-up bot, then the voice bot, which calls them. Leads are 80% more likely to respond if you reach them within 5 minutes vs. an hour later.

2) He built it by prompting Grok Bot. His first prompt: make a voice bot that learns from his email follow-up bot, which already knows his voice, and use @ElevenLabs. Learning from the follow-up bot was the most important part. It's what makes it sound like him.

3) He cloned his voice with a 3.5-minute voice note on his iPhone, uploaded to ElevenLabs. Then he bought a number on @twilio for 10 bucks and hooked it up to the Netlify form.

4) The first version spoke too fast and was too robotic, so he made it more conversational. On the call it asks your passport country, how much you want to invest, and when you want to move. Someone looking to invest $5,000 never gets on an attorney's calendar.

5) Every call is logged in ElevenLabs and pushed into @attio, his CRM. Now he's A/B testing scripts and even accents, because leads from Turkey, India, and Canada respond to different ones.

It turns away 10 to 15 unqualified leads a day. Every 30-minute consult with someone who isn't a fit is $200 wasted.

He couldn't afford an assistant to call every lead. So he built one that sounds like him.

His best line: "i have not gone into our CRM since we set it up. i just talk to grok and it just helps me figure out the next steps."

Vitalik：不建议用户匆忙把资金转移到新钱包

Vitalik发文称，不建议用户因AI可能加速密码学破解而立即迁移资金，但应减少对量子计算和AI都可能构成风险的密码学方案的依赖，重点关注ML-DSA、全同态加密（FHE）及格密码。

他表示，未来两年AI在数学领域的进展可能削弱格密码的实际安全性，因此在可行情况下应优先采用基于哈希的方案；隐私协议尽量不要将加密信息上链，多签钱包也更适合进行链下确认。

Vitalik同时建议，条件允许时可将资金存放在尚未发起过交易的新地址，但提醒用户谨慎处理迁移操作，避免因操作失误造成损失。其观点并不意味着现有密码学方案已被攻破，而是强调应提前评估AI带来的长期安全风险。
author: PANewsCN
quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

一早起来读到Justin呼吁全行业开启大逃难模式。把资产有序迁移到从未签过名的新地址，让公钥继续藏在hash后面。判断是ECDSA 可能在量子计算机到来之前就被经典算法攻破，最坏情况以月计。

依据主要是OpenAI 近期接连推翻了数学界长期默认的猜想。椭圆曲线结构丰富，Schoof，Frobenius，配对都是可以做文章的地方。高效的量子算法有时预示着高效的经典算法，Shor 未必没有经典版本。所以放弃一切带结构的假设吧。

以此作为假设，那风险其实更大呀。ML-DSA, FHE 这些被post-quantum solutions，同样可能在未来两年的数学里被削弱。

有意思的是，其实密码学的安全性从来没有被证明过。所谓128 位安全的真实含义是目前已知最好的攻击需要 2^128 步。这是一个关于知识边界的陈述，而不是关于数学对象本身。过去几年密码学层面的exploit都不是暴力破解的胜利。都是有人看见了一直存在但没人注意的结构。

这就是为什么数学突破对密码学的影响是无法预知得巨大。

算法突破不是平滑分布的。算力增长可以外推，一个尚未被发现的算法却没有先验可言。可能只改掉指数里的一个常数，参数加大一档即可。也可能改变复杂度的形态，让整类方案失效。两种情况在发生之前无法区分。

What a crazy time to be alive.
author: Leozayaat
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
Justin's bunker mode is a workaround for one design decision: on Ethereum and Bitcoin, the address is the key. To change the key you must move the money.

NEAR separates the two. An account is a name, keys are attached to it and can be added or removed in one transaction. The assets, the contracts, the history stay where they are.

So key rotation on NEAR is not a migration. You add a new key, you delete the old one. Since July 2026 the new key can be ML-DSA, post-quantum. If hash-based signatures become the standard, that is one more key type, same account, same one transaction.

The industry will spend the next years moving funds around. 

NEAR users have been doing this since July, in one click.

text:
Marc Andreessen (@pmarca) on founders taking psychedelics:

“I was describing this phenomenon we see in Silicon Valley where these guys get under pressure and they feel anxious and somebody tells them about psychedelics. 

They try it and they kind of come out the other end as a changed person. And they kind of come out much more at peace, but then they also tend to like quit their companies and they move to Indonesia and become a surf instructor. 

They just peace out. They're just done. 

There's been a whole bunch of examples of this and I was complaining to @hubermanlab about this and in true Huberman kind of wise Yoda style, he's like, "Well, you know, how do you know they're not happier? Maybe that was the positive outcome. Maybe the thing that was driving them to be a great entrepreneur was a fundamental level of insecurity. They had this kind of unsatisfied, neurotic impulse, and now, they're just satisfied.”

And I'm like, "Yeah, but their company, it's failing."

text:
I found Microsoft's announcements today to be pretty meh.

They copied Spotlight (who copied Raycast) with a bunch of quick action features that basically nobody will use.

Surface Laptop Ultra is a dud for AI.
 
1TB storage only on the 128GB preorder. You can't even config an M5 Max MacBook Pro with that little. And no options for > 2TB? This is for AI devs? No, no it is not. 
 
Price roughly the same as the MacBook Pro M5. $5,899 for the Surface Laptop Ultra with 128GB and 1TB, $6,699 for the MacBook Pro with 128GB and twice the storage at 2TB. You might be able to swap in a 4TB SSD in to the Ultra, but it looks like it might be a tiny 2230 drive and consumers can't get 4TB in that size.

One advantage you get over macOS is full CUDA, but most CUDA devs would likely prefer to run a Linux system natively, not with all of Windows along with it.

Surface RTX Spark Dev Box will never sell in volume.

$5,999 for a 128GB Spark desktop is about $1,000 cheaper than NVIDIA current prices. But it runs Windows, so almost no one cares. The whole point of Spark is to run the same platform you're deploying to, nobody deploys AI to Windows servers. Sure, CUDA runs in WSL, but that's Linux inside Windows, so expect complexity and compatibility issues. I guess enterprise shops that run Windows might be interested, but they are famously cost-conscious and this is an expensive box. $5,999 is a lot of tokens.

Shower thought: is Microsoft saying cloud AI is insecure, not private, and expensive? How are they threading *that* needle with their enterprise customers? 🤔

It is good validation for the value of on-device AI, and "hybrid intelligence" is good marketing from Nadella. 

Apple has been completely, totally silent on on-device AI for business since one private business event back in June. (Right around when I left Apple and stopped working on AI and business!) 😀

text:
thought id do a little break down of what spend looks like for this, for the sake of transparency and execution. 

if you have found yourself doing a similar thing - you should be held accountable to a high level of execution when you're asking for 1000s of dollars in sponsorship. 

this to me is a given, out of respect to those giving you the money. 

so here is every single thing the sponsorship money paid for, and just some of the additional costs that have gone  into this silly little race. 

i raised $5,500. $200 of that got refunded because one sponsor couldn't get their artwork to me in time.

the big one was obviously the bike 

$4,996.73 quintana roo x-pr. priced at $4,828 [i got her on the labour day sale], came down to $4,345, then shipping and tax put it straight back up again. i literally emailed them asking for twenty dollars off because my card has a 5k limit and the price was sixteen dollars over it.

$152.65 pedals. isn't it crazy that bikes don't come with pedals. 

$349.83 jakroo custom suit. this is the one carrying most of the logos. THIS IS SO IMPORTANT, not only do i want to look good i want my sponsors to look good, i truly cant wait for the race photos.

$178.99 ekoi aero16 helmet. normally around $400. [if you havent guessed i LOVE a sale] i chose one that had good spacing for the logos to go on.

~$200 vinyl printing for the logos.

$5,878.20 total. and this is just the basics of what the sponsorship funds cover

oh and bike shoes $208.53

then theres training

$399 wahoo kickr, down from about $550 on prime day. i have nine weeks to get comfortable on a bike i have genuinely never ridden, so i'm going to be clocking hours on this thing indoors.

and that's still only the bike. race entry alone was $500, then theres coach plans, gyms, physio, and none of the swim or run gear, because i've been doing those two my whole life and that money went years ago. but in the next few weeks i'll likely be picking up the asics metaspeed. i run in one pair of hokas, and get new ones every 500 miles or so. my wetsuit was $224 which i got from the quintana roo sample sale.

so here why

i had genuine reason for thinking i could execute this and here is the actual reason i did it this way.

triathlon is an obscene sport to be mid at. every person you watch doing this full time is sponsored, that is the entire reason they're able to be there. and sponsorship basically does not exist for age groupers. theres a reason the average income for an ironman is $200,000. and yeah thats tough shit, skill issue, but fuck it. 

the only reason this worked for me is that i already have an audience on twitter. i'd rather say plainly that that's the unfair advantage than pretend i found a clever trick anyone could copy and i am fully aware of the fallout, do i agree with a lot of it, especially the outright disrespectful execution of some, not really my place to say, anyway.

what i can control is executing it properly for myself. nineteen brands put money on not just my bike, but on me. that's trust baby, i love trust, its very important to me, and the only way i know how to honour it is to make the thing look good, ride it hard, and show every receipt. [we're manifesting wc qualifing, but damn i need to get cozy on this machine first]

and yes, i know i went for an expensive bike. i sat with that for a while, i tried to find a bike on facebook marketplace, scoured all the second hand shops in LA. but she's not just going to carry me through this race, but many more after, she's going to be racing for many years to come.

i have truly fallen in love with this sport and training and the person im becoming on this journey, its phenomenal what the human body and mind can do. 

eternally grateful, love win

梳理一下本轮目前为止的主线逻辑：

山寨：
1、真实营收/回购/RWA
受益于Hyperliquid将绝大部分收入用于回购并销毁代币，很多项目方也开始跟进，但需要注意区分项目是能实打实产生营收并用于回购，还是刷数据左手倒右手。

而由于这波RWA带动的链上交易热潮，许多相关基建设施的交易量、TVL、营收等数据也迎来了爆发式增长，再配合上述的回购销毁机制，促成了这波山寨季。而且不同于以往的是，这次很多代币的上涨是由数据增长->收入回购这个正向飞轮驱动的，代币真正开始对协议价值捕获。

代表性的币种是$HYPE，$UNI，$RAY，$LIT，新兴的几个龙头发射台$PONS，$STONK，$AI也可以归入此类。

2、隐私/AI
这条线相对来说更注重叙事而非数据，拉盘自然有大儒辩经，最典型的就是$ZEC，其他较强势的币种包括$NEAR（隐私交易、全链交易、纳瓦尔转推），$VVV（隐私AI，算力代币化）。

链上：
主要由股票代币化驱动，按几条链看：

Robinhood
主打的就是股票代币化叙事，因此也在第一波行情中跑出了非常多的金狗，由两大发射台$PONS和$AI领衔，也有$CASHCAT这种纯Meme。可以感受到Robinhood是汲取了此前其他公链的经验和教训的，交易所和创始人都大力支持链上生态的发展，也因此不像此前大部分公链成了一波流。

近期因为币股配对叙事，该玩的基本都玩了一遍，再加上其他几条公链也在发力，所以Robinhood链上行情算是进入了一个冷却期。

Solana
本来许多人认为这一轮缺少了顶级CEX支持的Solana会就此沉寂，但它还是凭借强大的链上生态复苏了，一方面有配对ZEC的$ZCAT，也带动了许多和代币配对的Meme，SOL成了这种类型的第一选择。另一方面有主打Social Trading的$Cate，通过推出Poorgoat这样的领头人物，加上不断增长的Holder数来发展。这两者都在没有上线顶级交易所的情况下就突破了100M市值。

而这背后最大的受益者就是STONK，最初主打币股配对的时候上面跑出来的代币寥寥无几，但是项目方持续更新，不断加入新的山寨币和股票配对，最终杀出重围，目前STONK的营收已经持续好几天超越了PONS。

BSC
首先是Flap推出币股配对，上面诞生了作为BSC币股Meme龙头的$Marscoin和东西合力的Meme$牛来。

之后Four跟上，本来$4Stock是非常有机会作为“币股飞轮”这个叙事的完美代表的，因为只有BSC生态具备促成币股Meme->DAT公司BNC->代币BNB->公链BSC这一闭环的完整条件，可惜他们非要推一个高控盘，把情绪打没了。

最近Genius也推出了自己的发射平台，与其他平台的税收分红机制不同，https://t.co/TUH1ja2Rvr的税收是直接用于购买股票，目标是进入董事会，从这里能看出团队是针对目前的叙事专门做了设计的，再加上Genius本身就是CZ担任战略顾问的交易平台，因此目前$Gstock也反超了$4Stock成为了BNC币股Meme的龙头。

具体操作上，之前我主要持仓的山寨是$Hype，然后加入了$Uni，现在准备等回调再买入一些$Near和$Ray，链上则是持续关注看有没有新的催化剂带动一波新的风潮出现。

text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

text:
The RILLY Framework

I've spoken to at least 50+ different groups trying to tokenize some form of yield and getting Yuzu to deploy into it. Making a post on this so it helps those trying to do so to have a better sense of whether they will find success. Also for everyone to have a sense of what we look out for at Yuzu Money. I would caveat by saying that our criteria at Yuzu is also extremely strict and has a big focus on the asset's robustness so it may not be the same for everyone but I'm pretty confident that if what you are trying to tokenize ticks all of the following you will be successful.

1) Robust. The asset needs have either a long track record showing that it never had any drawdown (or very little). If it doesnt have a long track record it needs to be issued or affiliated by a brand name entity. For e.g. Auto, Home, Prime by Figure.

2) Interest rate sensitivity. Please stop pitching bonds. Bonds have interest rate sensivities. They experience a NAV drawdown when rates go up (aka duration risk). Not to mention the many different intermediary fees. We are in a rate hike cycle. 2Y duration risk looped by 10x = 10% drawdown in 2 rate hikes. This is different from underlying duration of the asset; although it is related. I also highly recommend you read up on this concept before thinking about tokenizing any yield instrument if you are not familiar with it. 

3) Liquidity. The asset needs be easily redeemable or unwound. Ideally within a week (e.g. Ethena, Maple, etc). Maximum a month (mGlo by Fasanara). Reason being most of the TVL in DeFi comes from looping. Making your asset loopable is what gets you most of your TVL. See next point. 

4) Looping. It must be leveragable on Morpho or Aave. Being leveragable means you are either on Aave v3 or get a major curator (e.g. @SentoraHQ, @gauntlet_xyz, @SteakhouseFi, etc) to green light your asset. Anyone can be on Morpho, but not everyone can pass a good curator's due diligence.

4) Yield. Most of you get this in reverse. You think yield is the most important but it actually is the least. Yield just needs to be higher than 5% (most probably 6%) cause thats what the benchmark (Ethena and Maple) are paying but all of the above is the most important.

Wormhole is moving into a new phase. We are prioritizing a leaner and more asset-focused approach.

We are entering this next phase with one core belief. The main use case for blockchains has always been inherently financial. We are witnessing the indisputable rise of 24/7 markets, asset tokenization, faster settlement, and the democratization of finance.

Just a few weeks ago, we saw SpaceX’s extremely hot IPO launch onchain via Sunrise and tradable on Solana at essentially the same time as the NASDAQ. Since then there has been over $670M in volume onchain from the Sunrise launch of SPCX. Other listings have followed in fast succession: MU (Micron Technology) SNDK (Sandisk) and more. The gap is closing.

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
I've read this post 5+ times and I increasingly have trouble with the core point.

If ECDSA breaks without warning, we have so much more to worry about than our magic internet money. Internet security as a whole is gone. SSL/TLS gone, the internet is now transparent.

Not just internet security as well - a large portion of physical security would become irrelevant too. You can't have secure digital locks if encryption is dead. You can't secure surveillance footage if the gateway it's stored on can be wiped out on a whim.

We would have much bigger problems than "your magic internet money gets stolen." The floor would drop out of the global economy.

Most importantly - the answer to transparent encryption simply cannot be "hide your magic internet money" when the internet wouldn't exist anymore. You'd be relying on this technology coming back online, and not just that, you'd be relying on the tokens you stashed away being the relevant ones when it does.

I get the ~reasonable dooming here, but if we're going to doom you have to take it to its conclusion. You're going to be much better off investing in gold or cylindrical lead if your core hypothesis is "ECDSA could be broken within months"

text:
IMD by @surfcoderepeat wants an idea to become a working financial application through a network of AI agents.

Its bigger ambition is for those agents to earn enough to keep building, eventually supporting companies managed entirely by the network.

That starts with two connected pieces: Identity MD NFTs organise the workforce, while the $IMD token connects payments and incentives.

Each of the 2,000  NFTs represents one swarm seat* Holders connect a machine running the IMD daemon and supply AI inference, the computation behind answers and code. The NFT lets an agent contribute to the network, although owning one doesn’t guarantee profitable work.

Customers bring that workforce an objective, such as building a vault and its website. The system checks the request and breaks it into implementation, testing, review and delivery with pricing is 0.5 IMD per request, paid on @Ethereum through x402.

When that work produces a token-bearing launch, the agents can participate in its economics.

- 2% of the new token’s supply goes to wallets with accepted launch work,
- 8% is allocated per connected seat at admission.

The requester controls the remaining 90% with their value depends on what gets built and whether anyone wants it.

The same workforce can also answer oracle questions for applications.

With chain evidence, agents propose calculations at fixed blocks, and the deployer reruns the agreed calculation before signing. A contract can verify that signature and the agreement count.

POOL4 connects its trading activity to funding.

When selling pushes IMD inventory above the protocol-owned pool’s cap, excess tokens and proportional ETH are removed.

- 85% of that IMD is earmarked for burning
- 4.5% for stakers
- 6% for orchestrator bonding
- 4.5% for NFT inference nodes

Stakers receive sIMD shares with growing IMD backing. Bonding would convert reserved tokens into ETH for computation, but bonding and node payouts remain unfinished.

As of October 5, swarm deployment remains Sepolia-only, while published work includes imdUSD documentation and Ember World audits.

However, there are some concerns like shared AI mistakes, deployer-dependent signing and unaudited POOL4 contracts remain substantial risks, including documented owner powers to withdraw liquidity and sweep staked IMD.

The encouraging part is that each useful application can give people another reason to use IMD and bring more work to the swarm. If that demand becomes recurring, it could help fund the agents that build the next application.

There’s still execution ahead, but the foundation is taking shape: a workforce, a payment token and a growing set of experiments.

Turning those experiments into products people keep using would bring IMD closer to its ambition of an economy that sustains its own builders.

NFA. DYOR.

Creating a broadly accepted standard for agents to identify themselves to service providers, so that providers can adjust the way they interface with clients (as compared to human-based traffic).

quoted_text:
Something strange is happening with the GPT models. They've always had a number of serious drawbacks tied to RL, but they also had certain strengths, which have practically disappeared lately. These models have become incredibly dumb and everything has gotten really bad. To me they're now at the level of Grok 4.7 and Kimi K3, even Astra.

1. GPT models were always known for their logical reasoning and analysis, especially in Pro thinking mode. Now any task that requires thinking and coming up with something is completely beyond them. It's gotten so bad that even Sonnet 5.5 now handles these tasks much better.

2. The best bug hunting and code review in the world has become super unreliable. There's a huge number of false positives. Just a month ago they solved these tasks with 100% accuracy.

3. GPT models were among the best at following instructions. Now they blatantly ignore any directions or instructions, constantly get lost, and don't understand what to do. They go off course and do something entirely different. It gives off the vibes of Opus 4.7 after the nerf, and Opus 5. Impossible to use.

4. The best Computer Use in the world has become practically useless because of the problems described above. I never used to trust Claude with these tasks, but over the last 2 weeks I've noticed it's easier and faster for me to delegate computer use tasks to Claude.

4. A strange quirk has appeared: they never answer the question that was asked. Ask any question, even the most primitive one like 2+2=?, and it will write a whole essay on why it's possibly 4, but by the next paragraph it starts doubting itself and produces a lot of pessimistic content about a pile of conditions required to get 4, and at the end it always adds an ambiguous conclusion with proof that nobody in the scientific world actually knows for sure what the value equals. Try asking something more serious and you'll regret it 20 times over. It's easier to go to Haiku 4.5 than to talk to GPT.

5. GPT models were always autistic, with zero emotional intelligence. They were terrible at understanding your intentions. But now it's gotten even worse. It has practically stopped adequately understanding your requests.

6. The Codex app has gone from the best to the worst. Terribly slow and full of bugs.

Something has definitely been done to GPT. Astra and 6.1 Sol aren't working the way they should. And something strange is going on with the company itself too. Lots of fuss, empty hype, failed decisions, and an inability to focus on what the audience actually needs

quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
Fun to talk with @jgreze (@TownAI) and Deeni Fathia (@GammaApp) about building a consumer AI business 

These two teams are best-in-class in developing delightful, retentive products that individuals adopt...and then bring into work. 

My takeaways: 

- Consumers are unlikely to pay for AI directly (via subscription). But, using consumer as a low cost enterprise funnel can be very effective, especially if you have a product where the output is naturally shareable and is used to do meaningful work. 

- You can't serve everyone. Some highly technical users are going to want a level of granularity / dial tuning that doesn't make sense to provide. You can lean in to this in select areas of the product where the average user does care - for Gamma, this is selecting image models.

- For products that are adopted across a team, pooling tokens is one way to approach pricing. Employees will naturally have varying levels of adoption of AI tools, and allowing sharing across a team can feel more fair / give customers higher ROI (they'll be more likely to stay!) 

- The ecosystem resets every 2-3 months, so you need to be always reinventing yourself as a company. Gamma (which has more than 100M users) just rebuilt and relaunched its product in ~3 months to better serve how people are looking to tell stories with AI now. 

- Trying to beat the labs at their own game is often a mistake. Leaning into a specific angle that you feel unlocks the market (for Town, this is multiplayer) or a specific type of customer is often better than trying to take the same approach with fewer resources.

text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"
