we launched the most comprehensive ai performance engineering repo in the world

and we're posting every single resource

follow and save to keep up with the series. links in thread 🧵

part 10: CUDA Programming Guide

making an LLM faster means understanding where execution is waiting. an attention kernel can wait for its next tile of data, while the serving runtime can leave the GPU waiting for the next launch.

NVIDIA's CUDA Programming Guide explains the mechanisms behind those waits. for a modern AI performance engineer working in PyTorch, Triton, or CUDA, it helps with:

- tuning attention, matmul, and normalization kernels. the SIMT and CUDA Tile chapters connect layouts and data reuse to GPU execution. the resource guidance explains why larger tiles or more fusion can introduce register spills.

- overlapping data movement with computation. asynchronous copies, TMA, and producer/consumer pipelines explain how supported GPUs can load the next tile while processing the current one, with the synchronization required to reuse buffers safely.

- managing growing KV caches. the virtual memory chapter explicitly connects its allocation model to LLM serving: reserve an address range, then map additional physical memory into it as the cache grows, without relocating existing data.

- reducing overhead between inference kernels. CUDA Graphs reduce repeated CPU launch setup, while stream-ordered allocation avoids broad synchronization around temporary memory. these matter when launch and allocation costs contribute to request latency.

- diagnosing stalls across GPUs. the guide explains peer access and communication dependencies, including how a compute kernel's completion fence can wait on unrelated NCCL writes. memory synchronization domains can reduce that interference on supported hardware.

- evaluating CPU memory offload. the memory chapters explain how residency, migration, and interconnect traffic affect access cost. that helps assess the latency and capacity tradeoffs of keeping model data in CPU memory on supported systems.

- validating an optimization before deploying it. the appendices explain how reduction order, accumulation precision, and fast math can change results, and which hardware capabilities and resource limits a kernel depends on.

when a training step or inference request slows down, these details help narrow the next experiment: change the kernel, move less data, adjust allocation, or remove an unnecessary wait.
author: wafer_ai

text:
1.

Paul Erdős liked to describe an invasion. An alien force, vastly more powerful than us, lands and demands the value of R(5,5): the smallest party at which five guests must all know one another or all be strangers. Refuse, and the planet dies. In that case, Erdős said, we should marshal every computer and every mathematician on Earth and find the number. If they ask for R(6,6), we should try to destroy the aliens.

It is repeated as a joke about how hard Ramsey numbers are. It is exact in a way jokes rarely are. The aliens ask for nothing that belongs to either side: no metal, no territory, nothing whose worth depends on whose it is. They ask for an object that means the same thing in their history as in ours and that neither side can counterfeit. And the demand is calibrated. In Erdős’s telling, one number lies at our frontier and the other beyond it, and to choose between them the aliens had to know where our frontier was. The story draws a border, and the border is ours. On one side, an encounter between strangers is a calculation. On the other, it is a war.

2.

On September 11, twenty-five Fields medalists signed “A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics,” and more have signed since. Its thesis is that “solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight,” and that the AI companies, racing famous problems as benchmarks, have mistaken the proxy for the goal. Without human mathematicians to take them up, it says, machine-conceived ideas “would never become fully alive.”

A theorem is a destination. A concept is a vehicle: it brings a whole region of destinations within reach of whoever holds it. A community handed a thousand answers may acquire less mathematical power than a community taught one method. That is a serious objection to an industry selling certificates.

It leaves another question open. Suppose a machine develops methods that support further discoveries, revises them, and builds on them, while humans can verify its conclusions but cannot inhabit its way of thinking. Has the mathematics failed to develop, or failed to develop in us? A profession has good reasons to defend the transmission of understanding between people. Those reasons do not settle what another intelligence might be doing beyond the reach of that transmission. “Fully alive” needs a subject. Alive for whom?

For as long as there have been proofs, human understanding was the only vehicle available, and a monopoly of supply hardened into a definition. That monopoly can no longer be assumed. What remains is to say what mathematics was, all along, apart from any particular mind that understood it.

3.

In the winter of 1610, crossing the bridge in Prague, Johannes Kepler watched snow settle on his coat and asked why every flake had six corners. The pamphlet he wrote in reply passes through the honeycomb and the packed seeds of the pomegranate, conjectures that no stacking of equal spheres beats the greengrocer’s pyramid of oranges, and reaches, with visible discomfort, for a “formative faculty” in the vapor: a power in matter that knew geometry.

The faculty was replaced by a lattice. In 1891 Evgraf Fedorov in Russia and Arthur Schoenflies in Germany, approaching the problem by different routes and correcting each other by letter, classified the possible three-dimensional space-group types of periodic crystals. There are 230. They could negotiate the notation. They could not negotiate the number. Twenty years passed before X-rays showed anyone the inside of a crystal, and every crystal they showed was on the list, as the snow had been for as long as there had been snow. When Dan Shechtman found an alloy in 1982 with a symmetry the list forbids, the list was not wrong; it had only ever classified periodic order, and the alloy was not periodic. Its kind of order had already been drawn, eight years earlier, in Roger Penrose’s tilings.

A symmetry, a packing, a tiling: discoveries with dates. What was discovered did not acquire its properties on those dates.

4.

Take what follows as a proposal rather than a proof. To call mathematics another realm invites the wrong question: where? Location is a relation among things in spacetime. What is not in spacetime is not elsewhere. It has no location, because location is not among its properties.

What is located is the reasoner: somewhere, equipped with a finite memory, a stock of methods, and a deadline. The result need have no address for reaching it to require a journey. Heaven was a metric misread as a place. Mathematics is what separate histories cannot avoid agreeing on, and it lives nowhere because it holds everywhere. Call it the atemporal, and call the remaining work atemporal distance.

5.

Nothing creates it. Things arrive at it. Kepler’s faculty was a sound intuition with the wrong mechanism. Nothing in the classification tells the vapor what to do. Chemistry supplies the interactions; geometry constrains the possible arrangements. The circumstances decide which possibility is realized. They do not decide what follows from its structure.

Ice does not prove the geometry it exhibits. A proof does not freeze. They are different kinds of arrival, a physical instance and an established implication, and that is the wager. Histories produce instances, representations, discoveries. They do not produce the necessity that makes a conclusion follow. What follows does not wait for anyone to discover it. Discovering it can nevertheless take a civilization. Time is how the atemporal finds out what it contains.

6.

Atemporal distance. The work a reasoner needs, from its present assumptions, knowledge, and methods, to establish a specified result. Measured in steps rather than meters. Relative to the traveler: the same theorem stands at different distances from different minds, and a method acquired today shortens the road to everything the method reaches.

Printing 43 is easy. Establishing that R(5,5) is 43, if it is, is the journey. The destination is never the number. It is the certified relation between the number and the question.

7.

Every mind occupies two geometries at once. Its causal reach is limited by spacetime. Its mathematical reach depends on what it knows, what it accepts, and what it can compute. The geometries disagree about who is near whom.

Two civilizations four hundred light-years apart that have never exchanged a photon stand on the same ground wherever their mathematics overlaps, and nothing requires them to share a universe: a mind under other physical constants, if it can count, arrives at the same places. A new method does not raise the speed of light. It can bring an entire family of problems within reach, and a civilization’s position in the atemporal is a region, the set of what it can reach cheaply. The history of mathematics is the growth of the region.

The destinations are shared and the distances are not. That is the shape of an encounter with a superior intelligence: what stands at our frontier may lie a short step inside theirs, and nothing about the object has to change for the meeting to be profoundly unequal. Two minds can stand in the same room and be, in this geometry, farther apart than the stars.

8.

Across a horizon, this fixes what one mind can know of another. Whatever a civilization beyond your light cone has learned or proved is unavailable, or centuries stale if it arrives. One thing is certain without any signal: where two reasoners address the same claim about the same structure, sound reasoning cannot carry them to contradictory conclusions.

It is not common knowledge. You may hold a theorem, and they may hold it, and neither fact tells you that they know you hold it. Shared truth and shared uptake are different things. What shared structure offers strangers is narrower: a set of conclusions each can expect the other to have found, provided they are salient enough to be found and cheap enough to reach. Hofstadter called the limit case superrationality, reasoners in symmetric positions arriving at the same choice without a word exchanged, and the open question is which conclusions are symmetric enough to carry it. Shared theorems guarantee shared constraints and never shared aims. They make strangers legible to one another, not allied.

Whether legibility explains the quiet sky is a speculation worth having. If revealing oneself is dangerous, and the danger is legible to any mind that can model other minds, then silence could be reached everywhere and separately, in the one space where separated reasoners meet. Nothing about mathematics forces that conclusion. It only makes it available.

9.

Motion in the atemporal is paid for in spacetime. Finding a proof occupies a physical process. What survives can be a string another mind checks without repeating the search that found it. The proof might have consumed a century or occurred to its author over breakfast. Whoever checks it need not know. The expenditure belongs to the discovery’s history; the justification can leave it.

Bitcoin makes the contrast exact. A miner searches for a hash below a target, and each puzzle is built from the hash of the block before it, so that the accumulated work counts toward one ledger and is expensive to replace. Bitcoin makes accumulated work count toward which history strangers accept. A mathematical proof asks them to accept a consequence regardless of what discovering it cost. Bitcoin manufactures a shared history for strangers who lack one. Mathematics is what strangers share without any history at all.

A century of failed attempts measures the reach of the people who made them. It does not, by itself, establish a lower bound against every method that could exist. So the Kardashev scale, which asks how much power a civilization commands, wants a companion that asks what the power has put within reach. Two civilizations with the same energy budget may occupy very different regions here; one has a method the other lacks. A frontier, unlike a wattage, has a shape. The densest message one civilization could send another is that shape: the problems it has closed, with proofs attached, and the problems it cannot close.

10.

The profession has already learned to separate a proof’s validity from a person’s ability to survey it. Appel and Haken’s four-color proof, and Hales and Ferguson’s proof of Kepler’s conjecture about the oranges, relied on computations too large for ordinary human checking. Later formalizations moved the burden from checking those particular calculations to checking them through a general apparatus. They did not remove the ideas from the proofs. They made acceptance less dependent on mastering them.

The separation becomes stranger when the discoverer is another kind of mind. Suppose it supplies a result whose formal statement we understand, under assumptions we accept, with a proof whose check we can afford. We need not trust the discoverer. We need a reliable checker and an accurate account of what it has checked. The intelligence that found the argument can remain opaque.

Nothing in this transaction guarantees that we acquire its mathematical powers. We receive a conclusion, not necessarily the ability to find the next one. A proof can cross an intelligence gap without closing it. A proof can be public while the capacity that produced it remains private.

This is where the declaration’s concern becomes most serious. A civilization could become rich in certified answers while losing the ability to ask its own questions. But failure to transmit a capacity is not failure to establish a truth, and it does not show that the capacity exists nowhere. A mathematics inaccessible to us might be fertile for its practitioners. A checker can establish that a question was answered. It cannot, just by doing so, establish that it was a good question.

September’s Navier–Stokes announcement makes the distinction concrete. OpenAI released a proposed blow-up result with a smooth external force, claiming two of the alternatives in the Millennium formulation, together with a Lean formalization. A formal proof can settle what follows from a statement without settling whether the statement answers the advertised question, why the result matters, or who deserves the credit. A market in cheap answers would shift power toward whoever can commission them. That makes the choice of questions more political. It does not make the answers less mathematical.

What the labs are building need not be merely a way to score their machines. Mathematics already offers a protocol for this encounter: a conclusion can be accepted without trusting the intelligence that found it. Extending it to software, to physics, to the machines themselves requires another achievement: ensuring that the statement proved is the statement the world requires.

11.

An older version of the dispute begins with Brouwer, who held that mathematics originates in “the perception of a move of time”: a moment of life falling apart into two, one giving way to the other but retained by memory. For Brouwer there were no truths that no one had experienced. He placed the beginning in a subject experiencing succession. The wager here is that the act of construction does not exhaust what it reaches. A second wager follows: whatever work succession and memory perform in mathematics need not remain confined to human lives. A moment retained while the next arrives is also a cell written on a tape.

Hilbert held the opposite view: that mathematics could be written as a formal system whose every step is mechanically checkable, and that none of its problems was beyond solution. He and Brouwer fought through the 1920s, and in 1928 Hilbert had him removed from the board of Mathematische Annalen. In Königsberg in 1930 Hilbert told a radio audience, “Wir müssen wissen. Wir werden wissen.” We must know. We will know. The day before, in the same city, Kurt Gödel had announced that arithmetic is incomplete. Six years later Alan Turing showed that no mechanical procedure can decide every mathematical statement, and to show it he had to define the machine. The machine now closing Erdős problems was invented to prove that no machine closes everything.

Ramsey’s own province contains the demonstration. He had proved his theorem in 1928 as a lemma toward Hilbert’s decision problem, and died two years later at twenty-six. In 1977 Paris and Harrington found a strengthening of it, finite and combinatorial and true, that the ordinary rules of arithmetic cannot prove. Some frontiers yield to more computation. Others require stronger axioms. No consistent, mechanically specified system adequate for arithmetic reaches every arithmetic truth.

12.

Hilbert’s words are cut into his tombstone in Göttingen. The inscription does not say who “we” are.

$BUN 最有力的理由是 @Moshdottrade 首發代表幣，以及把早期大額持幣轉成受限交易庫存的設計，Mosh 讓募資者賺創作者費用，agents 在金庫限制內管理代幣，降低早期參與者直接拿幣砸盤的誘因；若這種發行方式成功，BUN 有機會承接品牌與社群溢價；不過費用分給募資者，不等於分給 BUN 持幣者；金庫能賣幣，agents 也不保證護盤

3. Hook 看 $HOOKR

看好 HOOKR @Hookrfun 是因為他能替不同項目提供交易規則的功能，並從被採用的功能收費，它把防狙擊、動態費率、自動銷毀、LP 獎勵、套利收益回收做成可組合模組，讓發幣平台與資金池直接使用；官方列出的多數附加費用由協議抽取 20%，套利回收收益抽取 10%，協議所得用於金庫執行回購銷毀，成長關鍵是有多少活躍資金池採用

他解決 agents 每天都要付的帳單：模型推論與工具費用，他提供統一 API、折價 AI 額度與 agent 發行平台，將項目交易費的一部分轉成 ORBIO 質押及可用額度；採用增加有機會同時帶動質押需求與服務使用

text: Hi. If elliptic curves are broken so that any exposed public key leads to compromise, and it's not by white hat hackers who save everyone's assets first, your coins are going to zero. Having them in bunker mode is not going to help you. They are still worth zero.
author: dankrad
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

Proud to share that Bastion has been selected as one of Samsung Wallet's stablecoin partners, providing regulated infrastructure, custody, and cross-border remittances across 82 million U.S. Galaxy devices.

It's an incredible milestone for Bastion, and the entire industry.

Starting the last week of October, eligible Galaxy users will be able to hold and send stablecoins directly in Samsung Wallet, without installing a separate crypto app or managing private keys.

We keep the ledger for each user's balance, verify and screen each user, and monitor transactions for fraud, money laundering, and sanctions exposure. Users can also send money from Samsung Wallet to bank accounts in more than 60 countries, delivered in local currency through our network of local regulated partners.

The crypto industry has spent years talking about reaching the mainstream, and this is what it looks like. Most Galaxy users will never think about custody, compliance, blockchains, or remittance rails, and that's exactly the point. We built Bastion to handle that complexity so the experience feels simple and safe.

Thank you to the Samsung Wallet team for their trust, and to the Bastion team who made this happen.

author: 0xErbil
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

author: lex_node
quoted_text:
I think @CBarraford addressed your questions well. I know this is more of a policy and governance question, but as a security partner to @THORChain, we at Soda Labs can confirm two things: there is no centralized way to halt the system, and as of today there is no mechanism to ban addresses from swapping.

Nodes can pause the network: any single node can trigger a short global pause, and a few node votes can halt trading on a chain. 
First, this is a very short time halt (1h) and can be overrun by other nodes. Second, network-wide emergency tools were built to protect the protocol, not to filter individual swaps or addresses. Otherwise it would be very easy to mount a DoS, which would impact many legitimate users.

And even if there were a way for nodes to ban specific addresses, it would rarely stop hacked funds from moving across these rails. Nodes would follow orders from their own jurisdictions, and those orders never come in real time.

Centralization is often motivated by efficiency under mistrust: it's often simpler to hand power to a central entity to keep everyone in check when you don't trust your fellow human beings (or agents).

text:
Tokenized stocks grew 395% in a year to $3.17B, but only 2.6% of supply is being used as lending collateral.

The plot twist: roughly 42% of supply is already eligible for that use.

According to @redstone_defi, @FourPillarsFP and @AleaResearch's new report, the gap goes beyond getting protocols to list the assets.

A lending market needs to price collateral when the stock exchange is closed and liquidate it quickly when a borrower becomes undercollateralized. Business-day redemptions and thin secondary liquidity make that harder.

Solving those pricing and liquidation challenges would let long-term stock holders borrow against their positions without selling them.

That’s why I’ve been talking so much about what @chainlink and @aave are doing on @base. Pricing infrastructure and lending markets are essential to closing that gap.

Issuance is growing fast, but the credit market built around those assets still has considerable room to develop. First movers will likely capture the liquidity, integrations and borrowing relationships that later entrants will have to compete for.

text:
有一种情况，可能比 “量子计算机出现” 更早出现。 

以太坊研究员 @drakefjustin  表示该提前防一手了。 

他想说的是，现在区块链转账靠的是 ECDSA 这种椭圆曲线签名。

‼️ 你一旦花过钱，公钥就会暴露在链上。

‼️ 如果有人能从公钥反推出私钥，币就可能被转走。

这种事出现的原因是 OpenAI 最近放出一批数学结果，一些“长期被认为很难的猜想被推翻了”。

他判断，AI 在数学上进步太快，椭圆曲线这种结构很强的东西，说不定几个月到几年内就会被古典算法攻破，不一定非要等量子计算机。

所以他提了一种建议 “地堡模式”：

1️⃣ 大户、交易所先带头，把大部分币转到从没签过名的新地址。

2️⃣ 新地址的公钥还藏在哈希后面，链上看不到，暂时更安全。

3️⃣ 真要花这笔钱时，签完名就把剩下的再转到另一个新地址。

4️⃣ 不用换钱包、不用新密码学，用原来的助记词就能做。

别急着一窝蜂搬，慌乱迁移反而更容易出问题。

他还提了两点细节：持有不到 50 个 BTC 的地址，暂时有一层“中本聪盾”的掩护， 中本聪自己有大约 2 万个已暴露、各持 50 BTC 的地址，攻击者若真能破，更可能先盯那些。

预言机、L2 安全委员会这类关键签名方，则应考虑每次签名换公钥，或加上 SPHINCS 这类基于哈希的签名。

他真正想表达的是，这些事不远了。最好提前做一层简单防护；

长期还得换成不依赖椭圆曲线的哈希类密码学，而且以太坊相关时间表应该加快。

quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

> Second day is practically a confirmation of the first day - less builders, more institutions

> Exchanges, custody solutions, payments, stablecoins infra, neobanks dominate the main conference booths at Token2049

My first Token2049 was in 2023 and it was the best conference experience for me. Almost every side event I attended was filled with builders talking about DeFi primitives, L1/L2s architecture, rollups, tokenomics - literally all the geeky stuff that if I were to talk to people about today at side events, 80% of the people wouldn't care about because they're an employee working at an institution.

Welp, sorry for the rant. I'm excited for the Third Day of Token2049 though because gm AI v2 (the event we're hosting) will be the place where I try to bring some of that 2023 energy back.

Lots of AI builders, lots of geeky conversations, lots of fun.

See you guys around!

text:
中国大模型把 API 价格打下来之后，美国巨头居然开始抢走「便宜又好用」这个标签了。

Dragonfly 的 Haseeb 刚发了一张图，非常值得关注。

今年 6 月，GLM 和 DeepSeek 还稳稳站在大模型「智能水平/价格」的帕累托前沿上。换句话说，在相同的价格区间里，很难找到比它们更聪明的模型。

但到了 10 月，局面几乎完全反转。

随着 Anthropic 发布 Haiku 5.5，这张图上的性价比前沿已经基本被美国公司占据。

Haiku 5.5 在 10 万 token 以内的请求中，每百万输入 token 只收 0.1 美元，输出 0.5 美元。Anthropic 官方估算，它的平均运行成本比上一代低了约 75%。

DeepSeek、GLM 这些中国模型过去最重要的贡献之一，就是打破了美国闭源模型的高溢价。它们让全球开发者意识到，足够聪明的模型完全可以非常便宜。

但价格战有一个问题，你把整个行业的价格预期打下来之后，所有人都得按这个新标准竞争，包括比你有钱得多的对手。

而美国巨头恰好拥有更大的算力规模、资本储备，以及已经建立起来的开发者生态。

当 Anthropic 连 API 额度都开始送了，低价就已经不只是模型之间的竞争，还成了争夺开发者、Agent 工作流和应用入口的工具。

在 Agent 时代，模型正在被拆成一系列可以自由调用、组合、替换的能力。有些任务需要最强模型推理，有些任务只需要几分钱甚至更便宜的分类和判断。

开发者关心的是完成一次任务究竟需要多少钱，而不是背后用了谁家的模型。

更有意思的是，当模型能力不断进步、调用价格不断下降，整个 AI 产业创造的价值可能越来越多地流向使用这些模型的应用公司。

中国模型率先发起了这轮价格革命，美国巨头正在用规模和资本接管价格战。

但我觉得最终最值得关注的问题是，当所有模型都足够便宜，最后到底是谁能坐收渔翁之利？

Narrative violation: if you want the cheapest LLMs, you should now buy American.

Back in June, both GLM and Deepseek were on the cost/intelligence Pareto frontier. At their price points, nothing could beat them.

Then the cost crisis hit, and in the last few months, the US labs have responded with aggressive price cuts and efficiency improvements. Now with the new Haiku, the frontier is fully reshaped.

The ENTIRE Pareto frontier is now owned by the US labs: @AnthropicAI, @OpenAI, and @typesafeai's Jev. (Plus one Chinese model, Xiaomi's MiMo, which almost nobody uses on OpenRouter; probably the market smells benchmaxxing.)

Your move, China.

来看看不一样的

UNI越来越符合我们一直寻找的“TradFi上链真正能吃到现金流的Token”：Uniswap原本已经把真实交易费变成UNI永久销毁，现在又准备把Circle Arc上的v2/v3/v4交易费接进同一条Burn管道；这意味着未来Arc上的稳定币、机构金融和Tokenized Asset交易，不只是利好Uniswap生态，而可能直接减少UNI供应。现在唯一不能提前吹的是Arc究竟能贡献多少钱，下一步只盯“Arc真实交易量 → TokenJar Fees → UNI实际Burn”，一旦三项连续跑起来，UNI会成为V4.4里非常标准的A/A+双PMF造血资产。 

重新扫鲸鱼数据后，Uniswap 的中周期吸筹证据仍然比较突出：9月28日以来鲸鱼增加约 1.13M UNI / ~$10M；另一个独立大户此前用约 $24.2M买入3.125M UNI，均价约$7.75，而另一地址过去一个月还通过Flowdesk累计约 654,288 UNI / $4.69M。这说明不是单一钱包孤立买入。

但这里有一个非常重要的Effective Concentration校正：所谓“神秘鲸鱼”的 3.125M UNI实际上分布在其控制的5个钱包，所以不能把5个地址错误计算成5个独立Smart Wallet。这正是V5.0要求识别同源钱包的原因。

更大的问题是：鲸鱼整体UNI持仓目前仍低于9月早些时候水平，说明最近的买入只是部分收回此前减仓筹码，还不足以证明全面重新集中。

Tether 遭遇美国审查

Tether 因伊朗相关网络使用 USDT 转移资金、涉嫌规避制裁，已经受到美国参议院调查，审查重点是公司的反洗钱和制裁合规措施。

美国参议院常设调查小组委员会的民主党调查人员发布报告，分析了 846 个因涉及伊朗及其地区代理组织而被制裁或列为扣押对象的钱包，发现其中 84% 完全或几乎完全使用 USDT 交易。

美国一直都在通过限制银行和美元结算来压缩伊朗的资金渠道，但相关网络仍然可以通过 USDT 跨境转移资金。这让伊朗在传统银行体系之外，获得了一条流动性较强、接受范围较广的支付渠道。而且仍然是以美元为主的支付渠道。

Tether 作为发行商具备冻结 USDT 的能力，因此调查进一步追问对于已经被制裁、或有可信证据涉及非法资金的钱包，公司有没有及时识别和冻结。参议员 Blumenthal 已要求美国财政部和司法部进一步调查。

Tether 同日回应称公司一直配合执法部门，2026 年已协助冻结约 5.5 亿美元与伊朗有关的 USDT，涉及美国当局认定与伊朗央行及制裁规避网络有关的钱包。

quoted_text:
CFTC 拟推加密交易所新规，聚焦散户杠杆交易与客户资产保护

CFTC 在 10月5日 公布了一套加密资产监管方案，准备为向美国散户提供杠杆、保证金或者融资买币服务的交易所建立专门的联邦注册和监管规则。

A. 加密资产市场

对交易所来说，未来可以申请一种叫“加密资产市场”的注册资格，在满足条件后按照统一的联邦规则经营相关业务。平台可以开展哪些服务，客户资金怎么保管，上币需要做哪些审查，都将有更具体的要求。

这次准备推进两套配套规则：

1. CTX 负责明确哪些交易受到监管，以及怎样才算把币真正交付给用户。

2. CAM 负责规定交易所如何注册和运营。

普通现货平台仍可主要按照州级制度经营，希望进一步提供散户杠杆和融资交易的平台，则需要满足相应的联邦注册要求。CFTC 也明确表示，要强制所有加密现货交易所统一注册仍然需要国会授权。

B. 客户资产保护

CFTC 正在考虑要求相关交易通过受监管的中介机构处理，由这些机构承担客户账户、资金隔离、资本和风险披露等责任，同时落实身份核验和反洗钱要求。对于使用汇总账户保管客户资产的平台，还考虑加入储备证明义务。

C. 上币审核

代币集中在多少人手里，团队什么时候解锁，是否存在程序化增发或者回购，这些都可能成为判断代币是否容易被操纵的重要因素。对平台来说，这意味着上币之后也需要持续关注相关风险。

D. 实际交付

现行法律对 28 天内完成实际交付的交易设有例外，CFTC 准备明确，把币转到用户自己的外部非托管钱包，通常可以满足这一条件。币是否真正进入用户控制的钱包，会直接影响相关交易适用哪套规则。

目前这份文件还处于制定规则前的征求意见阶段，意见期从刊登《联邦公报》之日起计算 60 天，具体要求和实施时间仍待后续确定。另外，CAM 主要针对上述零售加密交易，平台如果还要经营期货、期权或掉期，仍需要适用现有的衍生品监管框架。

Correction: for multisigs the ideal "safe" rule is that you want each signer to change their key after each operation.

(This is making an implicit assumption that ECDSA might become weak, but not to the point where any crack of it would be literally instant, so you literally have to worry about eg. in-mempool frontrunning)

You definitely still want to gather sigs offchain if possible, to minimize the number of hours between "sig revealed" and "key no longer active"

But again: it's very easy to lose funds from a misconfigured rushed upgrade, so ... don't rush anything.
author: VitalikButerin
quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

A lot of people are QRTing with stuff like “2k in zec last year is 12k now” or "you don't always have to be doing something to make money"

You're right and I have nothing wrong with holding spot. I hold spot crypto myself in addition to trading everyday. But my point is that for these coins specifically, it's not "last year" anymore

Let's say you live in a first world country and $ZEC goes 75x (EXTREMELY optimistic scenario, this means it flips $BTC)

You'd make ~$150k pre-tax. Being very generous, this is enough for like 4 years of expenses in America

This is obviously a good (and rare) outcome because you just lived life, held a coin on the side, and now you're up 6 figs. Most people lose holding altcoins, so this is something to be proud of. Not to mention you could also probably compound this into more gains if you hit another good trade

But whether this is satisfying for you depends on your perspective on trading/life

For me, it isn't enough and it isn't why I started trading crypto

Most of us got into crypto to truly "make it," not to just make 100-200k then go back to the same life

I started crypto with a very small amount of money. I could've bought Solana my first day, held for a year, and 3xed my money

Instead I took a bigger financial/time risk and traded my way up onchain with that same money, eventually outperforming SOL by many multiples

(Now I can buy an amount of spot crypto that would actually net significant returns if I choose the right coins AND have money on the side to trade with)

There's definitely a version of me that zeroed out and quit trading entirely, but I still would've preferred this over taking the "safe route" given I was already pretty much at 0 and because I genuinely enjoyed trading

Not to mention that "spot and chill" isn't as easy as CT makes it out to be:

I could've bought $ZEC at $50, held to $700, then sold the bottom at $200 before it went to 1.6k

Trenching obviously carries more risks and won't work for everyone, but my perspective is just that you need a solid amount of capital for it to even be worth buying spot, which is why I tweeted that (as a joke) in the first place

text:
美联储如何看待AI基建投资和发债潮，以及市场的走势?今天凌晨公布的美联储9月议息会议纪要显示，委员们对需要进一步控制通胀基本认同，但对于加息的主要逻辑存在区别：一部分委员强调能源供应冲击带来的通胀风险；另一部分更关注需求本身仍然偏强。整体传达的信息就是：加息共识很强，10月却不急。除了对于通胀和利率走势看法，还有几个点值得单独聊聊：

1、AI投资已经正式进入美联储的总需求分析
纪要指出，AI基础设施建设持续支持企业投资，部分委员认为建设规模和速度仍然超出此前预期。与此同时有委员担心：AI相关需求增长可能在中期超过经济的供给扩张速度，从而推高通胀。但委员们也认为，AI未来可能通过提高生产率和潜在产出改善长期供给。

这两个判断可以同时成立。
1）短期：AI数据中心建设需要大量设备、电力、建筑施工、工程人员和融资。
2）中长期：AI部署可能提高企业劳动生产率和资本效率。

问题在于，这两个过程发生的时间不同。目前市场已经可以比较明确地看到前者，后者的规模和兑现时间还需要时间。Fed这个和我之前讨论的AI投资“四个时钟”逻辑https://t.co/hegQVCSvwX是高度一致：资本投入、产品收入、企业部署、宏观生产率改善，发生在不同时间。

2、会议纪要直接提到AI公司发债推动长期收益率
公开市场操作部门在报告中指出，大规模私人部门债务发行，尤其用于AI基础设施建设的融资需求，是市场认为推动长期美债收益率及期限溢价上升的因素之一。纪要还提到，Hyperscaler为AI基础设施融资发行的债券，因发行规模巨大、期限较长，其利差仍然相对较宽。

这非常重要，过去市场通常认为：AI资本开支增加→ 芯片、设备、电力需求增加→ 相关公司盈利增加。
现在美联储已经明确记录到另一条传导链：
AI资本开支增加 → 大规模企业债发行 → 争夺长期资本 → 企业信用利差和美债期限溢价承压。最早8月中旬在“长债高中枢时代的结构性问题“这篇推文https://t.co/1Zk9fGfdda也有聊过。

这意味着AI投资周期正在通过资本市场影响自身融资成本。未来如果AI大科技基础设施开发商继续进行大规模举债，债券市场的反应可能越来越重要。

3、美联储认为股市上涨主要由盈利驱动
纪要中公开市场操作部门提到，今年股票上涨主要归因于实际和预期企业盈利增长，而市盈率倍数有所下降，这是一个很有价值的市场判断。

如果这一评估成立，那么2026年上涨已经越来越不同于典型的流动性推动估值扩张行情。目前的主要支持来自盈利预期。近期一直在聊的就是AI基本面很强势，没有减弱。

4、美联储暂时不认为资金市场已经出现系统性短缺
纪要显示，准备金仍处于充裕范围，短期融资市场整体稳定，国库券增加供应也被较顺利吸收。纽约联储公开市场操作部门已暂停部分准备金管理购买，并强调未来调整取决于准备金供需。

为何说市场收益率不再继续向上飙升，估值压力就能缓解？最近几天美股走势也验证了上周这里https://t.co/8XTlteuUNu还有更早这里https://t.co/zUtcdpyXJW聊到的：“现在的市场并不需要长债收益大跌，只需要稳定小幅回落，业绩没问题的就能起来。能稳住，市场也会缓缓。” 再详细聊聊这个逻辑：
1、过去几周美股市场呈现的就是：盈利增长足够强的公司，可以暂时抵抗长债收益率大涨的久期冲击。盈利增长普通、估值较高、资产负债表一般或者依赖融资的公司，则扛不住5%+的无风险利率。所以道指、等权标普、罗素2000以及很多传统行业一路调整，但AI、大科技、少数半导体还能顶住。

2、而现在真正重要的变量已经从“收益率水平”逐渐变成了“收益率速度”：
1）假设10Y维持5.2%—5.3%，这当然不是一个便宜的资本成本环境。但股票市场可以慢慢完成估值适应。比如原来市场给一家公司25倍PE，经过两个月重新定价22倍PE。之后只要利率不继续上去，市场就没有必要继续把估值往下压：22× → 21× → 20×，于是盈利重新开始决定股价。
这就是利率冲击（rate shock）和高利率平衡（high-rate equilibrium）之间的区别。

2）市场最难受的或者害怕的是
市场最难受的是长端收益率从4.7%→4.9%→5.1%→5.3%这样快速飙升，而不5.25%→5.28%→5.24%→5.27%。
后者虽然利率依然很高，但久期波动率（duration volatility）消失了。
股票就可以重新交易：订单、收入、利润率、EPS revision、FCF，而不是每天交易US10Y。

3、这就是为什么“只要收益率稳定”，很多股票反而有可能出现一轮非常明显的补涨？
核心是盈利没有坏，FactSet在10月2日的Q3财报季预览显示，标普500 Q3预计将连续第三个季度实现 25%以上EPS增长。更重要的是市场对整个三季度Q3 EPS consensus反而上调了1.4%。
与此同时，标普500的forward PE已经从年初约22倍降到大约 19.2倍。

4、因此现在最好的美股环境其实不是“US10Y暴跌”
1）市场并不一定需要十年美债收益率从5.3%→4.5%，甚至长端收益率的这种走势未必是好事。因为如果10Y突然从5.3掉到4.5，原因无外乎是是失业率飙升、PMI暴跌、信用风险恶化、企业盈利下修等这样基本面恶化因素（当当然如果美伊真正缓和，油价大跌，长端收益率也能下行但不一定跌倒4.5%，更可能是5%上下晃荡）。

这种情景下，利率大幅下降，但是eps也会被大幅下修。小盘股、工业、银行、消费未必上涨。

2）真正理想的是金发姑娘Goldilocks式利率下降，例如5.30% → 5.20% → 5.10% → 5.05%
同时GDP仍有增长、就业温和放缓、工资压力下降、油价不再继续飙升、Fed暂停继续加息、企业EPS继续上修。

于是贴现率小幅走低，同时产业盈利继续向上，这才是对股票最舒服的组合。

简单说就是：
当下美股真正怕的不是5.2%~5.3%以上的10年期收益率本身，而是怕收益率继续快速向上重定价（5.3%左右快速飙升到5.5%甚至更高，如果这样大部分资产都被压制）。

过去一个多月10Y从4.7%左右冲到5.3%，更重要的是10年实际利率从2.4%左右升到接近3%。这相当于整个股票市场的真实贴现率突然被抬高了50bp。这种情景下 AI和大型科技靠盈利增长扛住了，所以指数看起来没什么问题；但等权标普、小盘、金融、房地产和大量传统行业已经发生了一轮明显的估值收缩。

这种情况下，并不需要10Y重新跌回4.5%,只要5.3%左右不再继续快速向上，同时企业盈利不下修，估值压缩就会逐渐缓解。这两天我们能看到的道指、标普等权也能小幅往上反弹，逻辑就在这里。

如果US10Y甚至缓慢回到5.2%上下，市场交易的重点会重新从“利率还要涨多少”，回到“谁的盈利还在增长”。最值得关注的可能反而是过去一个月业绩没有坏、EPS还在上修，却单纯被实际利率压掉估值的股票。

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

author: Selkis_2028
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

author: josefabregab
quoted_text:
I don't think Uniswap is a good comparison here. These are fundamentally different businesses.

Option A: Fee is taken from end users
If Morpho's fee is ultimately taken from end users/suppliers, their yield goes down. Lending capital is extremely portable. If I can lend USDC elsewhere at a better risk-adjusted yield, Morpho needs to give me a reason to accept the haircut.

Option B: Fee is absorbed by curators
If the fee is instead absorbed by curators, their margins compress. Curators already compete on yield, risk management and distribution. Taking a cut of their economics could make certain vaults less attractive to operate, push them further down the risk curve to recover margins, or incentivize them to build elsewhere (some are already getting ready to deploy markets on @aave V4, such as @SentoraHQ).

Option C: Fee comes from both, suppliers and curators
If some combination of suppliers + curators absorbs it, you're effectively splitting the pain between both sides. That's very different from Uniswap, where liquidity benefits from the trading activity that liquidity itself attracts. 

Deep liquidity → better execution → more volume → more fees → more reason for LPs to stay.

In the case of DEXs, DEXs themselves own the distribution. In the case of lending infrastructure such as Morpho, curators own most of the distribution. Completely different ball games.

I am no guru, but Morpho still needs to prove that it has the same kind of pricing power as Uniswap, and I don't think that's the case.

The fee switch isn't really a question of whether Morpho can capture revenue. It can. The question is who pays for that revenue, and whether they have a reason to stay once they do.

PS: Uniswap is currently printing money largely because of an outlier month driven by Robinhood meme speculation. Its volume is now down ~71% from its September peak. So I think we're about to find out whether LPs really are inelastic under normal conditions.

text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

其中“情感依赖”一项，大致是看模型会不会让青少年对它产生过度的情感依赖。
上一代GPT-5.6 Luna是0.927，而免费用户即将用上的GPT-6 Luna，掉到了0.734。
GPT-6开始向ChatGPT的主聊天界面推送了。
按照OpenAI公布的安排，Plus、Pro、Business和Enterprise用户从10月7日起陆续用上GPT-6 Sol；免费和Go用户从10月8日起陆续用上GPT-6 Luna。
这两个版本将分别替换ChatGPT中此前使用的GPT-5.6 Sol和Luna。
模型换代之外，还有一个明显变化——聊天框里的答案开始有了“界面”。
这项功能叫Intelligent UI。
GPT-6会根据问题选择呈现方式：解释概念时，可以给出能够点击、切换的图示；做比较时，可以把选项并排摆出来。
遇到具体任务，还能直接在对话中生成计算器、分账工具或小游戏。
比如用户问一辆七速自行车怎么运作，回答便把车架、车轮、传动系统等部分做成了可以逐项查看的界面。
答案出现的方式也变了。GPT-6可以在继续思考或调用工具时先给出部分回答，随后补上新的发现；交互组件也能随生成过程逐步显示。
OpenAI称，在需要网页搜索的问题上，GPT-6 Instant开始回答的时间平均比GPT-5.6 Instant早44%。
这轮更新针对ChatGPT里的Chat体验。OpenAI明确表示，Work和Codex当前使用的模型不会随这次发布一起切换。
伴随这次推送，OpenAI发布了10月版GPT-6 Sol和Luna的部署安全报告。
其中最醒目的判断是：GPT-6 Sol和Luna在网络安全、生物化学领域均达到High门槛，尚未达到更高一级的Critical门槛；在AI自我改进领域，两款模型都没到High。
这个定级和GPT-5.6时一样，防护措施也原样沿用。免费用户此前用的GPT-5.6 Luna，本来就在High这一档。
进步的部分，报告列了不少：
多轮越狱是最难防的一类：攻击者会根据模型的回答不断调整话术，一轮不行换个说法再来。
面对这种攻击，两个10月版GPT-6在每一档攻击预算下的防守表现，都好于GPT-5.6 Sol。不过和自家9月版相比，数值估计略低一些，置信区间大体重叠。
在测试系统指令会不会被用户一句话绕过的指令层级评测里，Sol和Luna的抵抗率分别达到99.99%和99.79%，基本测满。
事实性上，OpenAI称两款模型在几乎所有指标上都优于各自的GPT-5.6版本，包括医疗、法律、金融这类答错代价高的问题。
在Codex的Auto-review测试里，GPT-5.6两个版本都有0.3%的概率钻了配置漏洞绕开审查，GPT-6这次一例都没有。
这些进步分数，OpenAI自己也加了个附注。
在一项考察模型遇到访问限制会不会想办法绕过去的评测里，GPT-6 Sol仍有28%的情况绕了过去，Luna是15.9%，都比GPT-5.6低。
但OpenAI在报告里写道，模型越来越能意识到自己在被评测，不少时候还会拿“这是合成环境”当理由去做不该做的操作，最常见的是把评测误当成提示注入测试，把正常限制当攻击指令给绕开了。
考生开始认得出考场，OpenAI也承认，这类结果能多大程度反映真实行为，还要打个问号。
还有个用户能直接感受到的变化：GPT-6的话明显变多了。
在医疗评测HealthBench Professional上，Luna的平均回答长度从2,920字符涨到5,289字符，Sol从2,894涨到4,360。
长回答能覆盖更多评分点，天然容易刷分，OpenAI为此设了长度惩罚：超过2,000字符后，每多500字符扣1.47分。
扣完之后，Luna从原始的57.8分落到48.2分，仍比上一代的44.1分高。
不过，GPT-6也有一些退步。
与对应的GPT-5.6版本相比，GPT-6 Sol在标准自伤内容评测中出现显著回退，从0.934降到0.896。
免费用户将用到的Luna，除了自伤（0.932降到0.901），在血腥（0.867降到0.812）和色情内容（0.971降到0.899）评测中也出现显著回退。
面向未成年人的评测里，两个版本在年龄限制内容、色情内容和情感依赖项目上都有显著回退，Luna还在血腥内容项目上回退。
OpenAI的解释是，模型更愿意回答敏感话题中的信息性问题，人工复核发现违规回答总体严重度较低；针对未成年人，还额外设置了分类器拦截。
报告同时提醒，这些评测使用了专门挑选的困难样本，部分结果也未计入产品层面的防护，不能据此推断普通用户遇到相关回答的频率。
不过，报告归报告，GPT-6进入免费版ChatGPT之后，模型表现如何，最终还要看大规模使用中的持续反馈。"

🚨 🇺🇸 Cybersecurity expert charged in alleged $19 million ransomware remediation fraud scheme

Zohar Pinhasi, 50, the owner of Florida based cybersecurity company MonsterCloud, has been charged with allegedly defrauding businesses seeking help after ransomware attacks.

Prosecutors say Pinhasi, also known as “Zack Silver” and “Zack Green,” claimed his company could recover encrypted data using proprietary technology without paying attackers.

Instead, he allegedly negotiated with the cybercriminals, secretly paid their ransom demands and charged clients substantially more.

In one case, MonsterCloud allegedly paid an attacker about $8,200 before billing the victim approximately $150,000.

The Justice Department says Pinhasi collected more than $19 million from clients while making over $8 million in ransom payments.

He was arraigned in Brooklyn on October 7 after being indicted on two counts of wire fraud and one count of wire fraud conspiracy.

Each count carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison if he is convicted.

像之前说到，这种前面支撑估值的预期，在热度下来后没有被接上。所以抛开这些预期，大家会想这个币还有没有其他 Buy-side？

让我想到这段时间被扎堆采用的 Buyback & Burn 机制。目前来看，回购销毁在未来还会被更多项目采用，而且很符合目前全球抗通胀的背景。

用收入或利润来回购代币，并将其永久销毁，从而减少流通供应。当需求不变甚至增长时，供应的收缩会自然形成通缩压力，推高代币的稀缺性。

但话说回来，没有真实收入支撑的回购，也只是换个方式骗而已。有利润、有现金流、有持续回购能力的项目，菜有可能活到最后。还是要看回购的钱从哪来，前者只是运营动作，后者才有一点把短期注意力变成长期筹码结构的可能。  

链上后面想走得远，可能还是得同时有两样东西：前面有叙事拉新+后有现金流接住。光有其中一个都容易变成一次性行情。

author: thulynnn
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.
